concepts.name: Thermal radiation
concepts.statement: All normal matter at temperatures above absolute zero emits electromagnetic radiation, a conversion of the body's internal thermal energy into electromagnetic energy, and this emission is called thermal radiation.

concepts.name: Blackbody
concepts.statement: An object that absorbs all radiation falling on it, at all wavelengths, is a blackbody; at a uniform temperature its emission, blackbody radiation, has a characteristic frequency distribution that depends only on the temperature.

concepts.name: Kirchhoff's law of thermal radiation
concepts.statement: A body emits radiation at a given temperature and frequency exactly as well as it absorbs the same radiation; otherwise a body in a room at one temperature would grow hotter while the room grew colder, contradicting the second law of thermodynamics.

concepts.name: Stefan-Boltzmann law
concepts.statement: The total power radiated from one square meter of black surface, integrated over all emitted frequencies, goes as the fourth power of the absolute temperature.

concepts.name: Wien's displacement law
concepts.statement: The frequency at which a blackbody's emission is most intense is directly proportional to its absolute temperature, so the peak wavelength is inversely proportional to it.

concepts.name: Spectral energy density
concepts.statement: The energy density of blackbody radiation per unit frequency, so that ρ(ν,T)dν is the energy per unit volume carried by frequencies between ν and ν + dν.

concepts.name: Rayleigh-Jeans law
concepts.statement: Classical physics, treating the radiation in a cavity as oscillators each with energy k_BT, predicts a spectral energy density that grows as the square of the frequency; it agrees with experiment at low frequencies only.

concepts.name: Ultraviolet catastrophe
concepts.statement: Integrated over all frequencies, the Rayleigh-Jeans law predicts that a blackbody radiates infinite energy, an absurd prediction caused by the classical law failing at high frequencies and short wavelengths.

concepts.name: Quantization of energy
concepts.statement: Energy is quantized when a system can hold only certain discrete amounts of it, like a ball on the steps of a ladder, rather than any amount, like a ball on a ramp.

concepts.name: Planck's quantum hypothesis
concepts.statement: Planck assumed that the oscillating electrons in the walls of a blackbody can have only energies that are whole-number multiples of a quantum hν, so energy is absorbed and emitted in these discrete amounts.

concepts.name: Planck's constant
concepts.statement: The constant of proportionality h between the energy of a quantum and its frequency, 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s.

concepts.name: Planck's distribution law
concepts.statement: With the quantum hypothesis, the spectral energy density of blackbody radiation is 8πhν³/c³ times 1/(e^{hν/k_BT} − 1), which agrees with experiment at all frequencies and reduces to the Rayleigh-Jeans law at low frequencies.

concepts.name: Photoelectric effect
concepts.statement: Light shining on a metal surface can eject electrons from it; the energy of the ejected electrons depends on the frequency of the light and not on its intensity, which classical wave theory cannot explain.

concepts.name: Photon
concepts.statement: A quantum of electromagnetic radiation, a packet of light carrying the energy hν.

concepts.name: Stopping voltage
concepts.statement: The minimum retarding voltage on the collector plate that stops every ejected photoelectron from getting through, a measure of the electrons' greatest kinetic energy.

concepts.name: Work function
concepts.statement: The minimum energy required to extract an electron from the surface of a metal, characteristic of the metal.

concepts.name: Threshold frequency
concepts.statement: The lowest frequency of light that can eject a photoelectron from a given metal, at which the photon energy just equals the work function.

concepts.name: Einstein's photoelectric equation
concepts.statement: A photon gives all its energy hν to one electron, which spends the work function Φ to leave the metal and keeps the rest as kinetic energy.

concepts.name: Line spectrum
concepts.statement: A spectrum of discrete wavelengths: an excited gas emits light only at the wavelengths characteristic of its atoms, and a cool gas in front of a continuous source absorbs light at the same wavelengths.

concepts.name: Wavenumber
concepts.statement: The reciprocal of the wavelength, the number of waves per unit length, used as a unit of frequency in spectroscopy and usually given in cm⁻¹.

concepts.name: Balmer formula
concepts.statement: Balmer found that the wavelengths of the visible lines of hydrogen fit λ = b n₂²/(n₂² − 4) for integers n₂ greater than 2.

concepts.name: Rydberg formula
concepts.statement: The wavenumbers of every line of the hydrogen spectrum are R_H(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²), where n₁ and n₂ are integers with n₂ greater than n₁ and R_H is the Rydberg constant.

concepts.name: Rydberg constant
concepts.statement: The empirical constant R_H of the Rydberg formula, 109,737 cm⁻¹.

concepts.name: Spectral series of hydrogen
concepts.statement: The lines of hydrogen fall into series, each sharing one lower value n₁: the Lyman series in the ultraviolet (n₁ = 1), the Balmer series in the visible (n₁ = 2), and the Paschen, Brackett and Pfund series in the infrared.

concepts.name: de Broglie wavelength
concepts.statement: De Broglie proposed that any particle of momentum p has a wavelength λ = h/p, as a photon does.

concepts.name: Wave-particle duality
concepts.statement: Light and matter both show the properties of particles and of waves, depending on the experiment.

concepts.name: Interference and diffraction
concepts.statement: Waves passing through two slits or scattered from a regular array interfere, producing bright and dark bands that particles of classical physics would not produce.

concepts.name: Diffraction of matter waves
concepts.statement: Electrons and neutrons scattered from crystals produce diffraction patterns with spacings fixed by their de Broglie wavelengths, the experimental proof of matter waves.

concepts.name: Coulomb potential
concepts.statement: The potential energy of two charges a distance r apart is kQ₁Q₂/r, repulsive when the charges have the same sign and attractive when they have opposite signs, and the force is minus its derivative.

concepts.name: Instability of the planetary atom
concepts.statement: A classical electron orbiting a nucleus is accelerating and must radiate energy, so it would spiral into the nucleus; Rutherford's planetary atom cannot be stable.

concepts.name: Bohr's quantization of angular momentum
concepts.statement: Bohr postulated that the electron's angular momentum in its orbit is restricted to whole-number multiples of ħ.

concepts.name: Bohr model
concepts.statement: The electron in a hydrogen-like atom moves on circular orbits whose angular momentum is quantized, does not radiate while in an orbit, and emits or absorbs a photon only when it jumps between orbits.

concepts.name: Bohr radius
concepts.statement: The radius a₀ = 4πε₀ħ²/(e²m_e) = 52.9 pm of the smallest orbit of the hydrogen atom in the Bohr model.

concepts.name: Bohr energy levels
concepts.statement: In the Bohr model the energy of the nth orbit of a hydrogen-like atom is −Z²/n² times 2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ J, one Rydberg.

concepts.name: Rydberg formula from the Bohr model
concepts.statement: The frequency of the photon emitted when the electron drops from orbit nᵢ to orbit n_f is the energy difference divided by h, which gives the Rydberg formula with its constant in terms of e, m_e, ε₀ and h.

concepts.name: Standing-wave picture of Bohr orbits
concepts.statement: An orbit is allowed when a whole number of de Broglie wavelengths fits around its circumference, so the electron's wave closes on itself; this reproduces Bohr's quantization of angular momentum.

concepts.name: Heisenberg uncertainty principle
concepts.statement: The position and the momentum of a particle cannot both be known exactly: the product of their uncertainties is at least ħ/2.

concepts.name: Wave packet
concepts.statement: A wave localized in space, built by adding waves of many wavelengths; the narrower the packet, the wider the spread of wavelengths and so of momenta it needs.

concepts.name: Probability in quantum mechanics
concepts.statement: Where a single quantum particle will be detected cannot be predicted exactly; only the probability of detection at each place, which builds up as a pattern over many particles.

concepts.name: Sine wave
concepts.statement: The simplest wave is the one-dimensional sine wave, whose amplitude at position x and time t is A(x,t) = A_o sin(kx − ωt + φ).

concepts.name: Amplitude
concepts.statement: The maximum amplitude of a wave is the largest distance of the medium from its equilibrium position during one wave cycle, from the crest to the baseline.

concepts.name: Wavenumber (angular)
concepts.statement: The wavenumber k of a sine wave sets how fast its phase advances along x, 2π radians per wavelength.

concepts.name: Angular frequency
concepts.statement: The angular frequency ω of a wave sets how fast its phase advances in time at a fixed position, 2π radians per period.

concepts.name: Phase constant
concepts.statement: The phase constant φ fixes where in its cycle the wave is at x = 0 and t = 0.

concepts.name: Traveling wave
concepts.statement: A traveling wave moves through space and time, carrying energy from one place to another; on a rope it travels at constant speed and keeps its shape, so its displacement is y(x,t) = f(x − vt).

concepts.name: Wave velocity
concepts.statement: The velocity of a wave is the speed at which its shape moves along the medium, the v by which f(x) is shifted to f(x − vt).

concepts.name: Standing wave
concepts.statement: A standing (stationary) wave stays in one place, with crests and troughs at fixed intervals separated by nodes; it only vibrates up and down, and no energy travels along it.

concepts.name: Node
concepts.statement: A node is a point (or line) of a standing wave that does not move while the rest of the medium vibrates.

concepts.name: Antinode
concepts.statement: An antinode is a place of maximum oscillation in a standing wave, halfway between neighbouring nodes.

concepts.name: Classical wave equation
concepts.statement: The displacement u(x,t) of a one-dimensional wave, traveling or standing, obeys the linear partial differential equation ∂²u/∂x² = (1/v²) ∂²u/∂t².

concepts.name: Boundary conditions
concepts.statement: Boundary conditions fix what happens at the ends of the medium; for a string of length L held taut at both ends, u(0,t) = 0 and u(L,t) = 0 for all t.

concepts.name: Initial conditions
concepts.statement: Initial conditions fix how the wave is produced: the values of the solution (and its rate of change) at a starting time.

concepts.name: Partial differential equation
concepts.statement: A partial differential equation (PDE) involves a function of two or more independent variables and its partial derivatives; the wave equation is a second-order PDE in x and t.

concepts.name: Ordinary differential equation
concepts.statement: An ordinary differential equation (ODE) contains a function or functions of one independent variable and its derivatives.

concepts.name: Separating the variables of a PDE
concepts.statement: Assume the solution is a product of functions of one variable each, u(x,t) = X(x)T(t), substitute it into the PDE and collect each variable on its own side, turning the PDE into ordinary differential equations; sums of such solutions are solutions of a linear equation.

concepts.name: Separated wave equation
concepts.statement: Substituting u = X(x)T(t) into the wave equation and dividing by XT leaves a side in x only and a side in t only, so each equals one constant K, giving two ordinary differential equations.

concepts.name: Trivial solution
concepts.statement: The trivial solution u = 0 satisfies the equation and its boundary conditions but describes no wave, so it is ignored.

concepts.name: Exponential solutions of a second-order linear equation
concepts.statement: Trying y = e^{αx} in d²y/dx² − k²y = 0 gives α² − k² = 0, so α = ±k and the general solution is any linear combination y = c₁e^{kx} + c₂e^{−kx}.

concepts.name: Euler's formula
concepts.statement: A complex exponential is a combination of a cosine and a sine: e^{iθ} = cos θ + i sin θ.

concepts.name: Oscillatory solutions
concepts.statement: When the separation constant is negative, K = −p², the spatial equation is d²X/dx² + p²X = 0, whose general solution X = Ae^{ipx} + Be^{−ipx} can be written X = c₁ cos(px) + c₂ sin(px).

concepts.name: Quantization by boundary conditions
concepts.statement: Requiring X(0) = 0 and X(L) = 0 forces c₁ = 0 and sin(pL) = 0, so pL = nπ with n = 1, 2, 3, …: only solutions with specific wavelengths exist.

concepts.name: Spatial solutions of a string fixed at both ends
concepts.statement: The spatial part of the wave equation's solution for a string held at zero at both ends is X(x) = D sin(nπx/L), an infinite set distinguished by n.

concepts.name: Quantum number
concepts.statement: A quantum number is the integer parameter, introduced by the boundary conditions, that distinguishes the allowed solutions of a system from each other.

concepts.name: Temporal solutions of a string fixed at both ends
concepts.statement: With K = −(nπ/L)², the temporal equation is d²T/dt² + ω_n²T = 0 with ω_n = nvπ/L, solved by T(t) = E cos(ω_n t) + F sin(ω_n t); no boundary condition fixes E and F.

concepts.name: Normal mode
concepts.statement: Each solution u_n(x,t) = [G_n cos(ω_n t) + H_n sin(ω_n t)] sin(nπx/L) of the wave equation for a string held at both ends is a normal mode, a standing wave with its own frequency.

forms.latex: u_n(x,t) = \left[ G_n \cos (\omega_n t) + H_n \sin (\omega_n t) \right] \sin \left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{L} \right)

concepts.name: Fundamental and overtones
concepts.statement: The normal mode with n = 1 is the fundamental; each subsequent mode is an overtone, or harmonic.

concepts.name: Linear differential equation
concepts.statement: A differential equation is linear when the sum of any two of its solutions, and any af + bg with constants a and b, is also a solution.

concepts.name: Principle of Superposition
concepts.statement: The sum of two or more solutions of the wave equation is also a solution: where waves meet, the displacement at each point is the sum of the displacements of the waves singly, which is interference.

concepts.name: General solution as a superposition of normal modes
concepts.statement: Since the wave equation is linear and homogeneous, its total solution for the string is the sum of all its normal modes, u(x,t) = Σ_n [G_n cos(ω_n t) + H_n sin(ω_n t)] sin(nπx/L).

forms.latex: u(x,t) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left( G_n \cos (\omega_n t) + H_n \sin (\omega_n t) \right) \sin \left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}\right)

concepts.name: Frequencies of the normal modes
concepts.statement: The nth normal mode of a string oscillates at the natural frequency ν_n = ω_n/2π = nv/2L, so the more curved the mode, the faster it oscillates.

concepts.name: Wave equation in two and three dimensions
concepts.statement: The displacement of a wave in two or three dimensions obeys the wave equation with one second derivative per spatial direction, ∇²u = (1/v²) ∂²u/∂t², because the medium curves in every direction at once.

forms.latex: \dfrac{ \partial^2 u(x,y,t)}{\partial x^2} + \dfrac{ \partial^2 u(x,y,t)}{\partial y^2} = \dfrac{1}{v^2} \dfrac{ \partial^2 u(x,y,t)}{\partial t^2}
\dfrac{ \partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} + \dfrac{ \partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} + \dfrac{ \partial^2 u}{\partial z^2} = \dfrac{1}{v^2} \dfrac{ \partial^2 u}{\partial t^2}

concepts.name: Laplacian
concepts.statement: The Laplacian ∇² is the shorthand for the sum of the second partial derivatives in space, ∂²/∂x² + ∂²/∂y² + ∂²/∂z².

concepts.name: Wave vector
concepts.statement: The wave vector k points in the direction a harmonic wave in three dimensions is moving; its magnitude is |k| = √(k_x² + k_y² + k_z²).

concepts.name: Harmonic plane wave
concepts.statement: The three-dimensional wave equation has harmonic solutions u = A sin(k_x x + k_y y + k_z z − ωt) with ω = v|k|, the form of the fields in a radio or light wave.

forms.latex: u(x,y,z,t) = A \sin (k_x x +k_y y +k_z z -\omega t)

concepts.name: Modes of a rectangular membrane
concepts.statement: Separating variables with the edges held fixed gives the modes of a rectangular membrane of length a and width b, u = A_nm cos(ω_nm t + φ_nm) sin(n_xπx/a) sin(n_yπy/b), with one quantum number in each dimension.

concepts.name: Nodal line
concepts.statement: On a two-dimensional membrane the nodes are lines that do not move: straight lines across a rectangle, and diameters (angular nodes, at fixed angles) and circles (radial nodes, at fixed radii) on a circle.

concepts.name: Bessel function
concepts.statement: Bessel functions J_m are oscillatory functions that give the radial shape of the modes of a circular membrane.

concepts.name: Modes of a circular membrane
concepts.statement: The modes of a circular membrane, in polar coordinates, are u(r,θ,t) = J_m(λ_mn r) cos mθ cos cλ_mn t, with two quantum numbers m and n that play the roles of n_x and n_y.

forms.latex: u(r, \theta, t)=J_{m}\left(\lambda_{m n} r\right) \cos m \theta \cos c \lambda_{m n} t

concepts.name: Wavefunction
concepts.statement: The solution of a wave equation, a function of the space coordinates x, y, z and the time t, is called the wavefunction; for a particle it is the amplitude of its matter wave.

concepts.name: Reduced Planck's constant
concepts.statement: Planck's constant divided by 2π, ħ ≡ h/2π, introduced by Dirac because h occurs in most formulas with the denominator 2π.

concepts.name: Free-particle matter wave
concepts.statement: Replacing ν and λ in a traveling wave by E/h and h/p gives the wave of a particle of energy E and momentum p moving in the x direction.

concepts.name: Schrödinger equation for a free particle
concepts.statement: The wavefunction of a free particle, on which no force acts, satisfies iħ ∂Ψ/∂t = −(ħ²/2m) ∂²Ψ/∂x², which follows from E = p²/2m.

concepts.name: Time-dependent Schrödinger equation
concepts.statement: The wavefunction of a particle of mass m in a potential energy V that depends on position only obeys iħ ∂Ψ/∂t = [−(ħ²/2m)∇² + V]Ψ; the equation is postulated, not derived.

concepts.name: Stationary state
concepts.statement: For a conservative system, whose energy is constant, the wavefunction separates into a space-only factor ψ(r) and a phase factor e^{−iEt/ħ} of constant magnitude.

concepts.name: Time-independent Schrödinger equation
concepts.statement: The space-only wavefunction ψ of a state of energy E satisfies [−(ħ²/2m)∇² + V]ψ = Eψ: the total energy is the kinetic energy plus the potential energy.

concepts.name: Operator
concepts.statement: An operator is a rule for turning one function into another, as a function is a rule for turning one number into another; it is often marked by a hat.

concepts.name: Hamiltonian operator
concepts.statement: The operator of the time-independent Schrödinger equation, Ĥ = −(ħ²/2m)∇² + V, which corresponds to the total energy of the system.

concepts.name: Eigenvalue equation
concepts.statement: An equation in which an operator acting on a function gives a constant times the same function.

concepts.name: Eigenfunction
concepts.statement: A function that solves an eigenvalue equation of an operator; eigen is the German word for self or own.

concepts.name: Eigenvalue
concepts.statement: The constant that multiplies the eigenfunction in an eigenvalue equation.

concepts.name: Operator algebra
concepts.statement: Operators add and multiply by acting on a function in turn: (Â ± B̂)f = Âf ± B̂f, ÂB̂f = Â[B̂f]; the associative law holds, but the commutative law does not in general.

concepts.name: Commutator
concepts.statement: The commutator of Â and B̂ is ÂB̂ − B̂Â; the operators commute when it is zero, and then the order of operating does not matter.

concepts.name: Linear operator
concepts.statement: An operator Ô is linear when Ô(f + g) = Ôf + Ôg and Ô(cf) = cÔf for any constant c, real or complex; most operators of quantum mechanics are linear.

concepts.name: Hermitian operator
concepts.statement: An operator Â is Hermitian, or self-adjoint, when ∫f*Âg dτ = (∫g*Âf dτ)* for all functions f and g that obey the specified boundary conditions.

concepts.name: The Hamiltonian is Hermitian
concepts.statement: Integrating by parts twice, with the boundary terms vanishing, shows that the particle-in-a-box Hamiltonian satisfies the Hermitian condition.

concepts.name: Operators of observables are Hermitian
concepts.statement: It is postulated that all quantum-mechanical operators that represent dynamical variables are Hermitian.

concepts.name: Observables are eigenvalues
concepts.statement: Every experimental measurable a is an eigenvalue of a specific operator Â, Âψ = aψ; the eigenvalues are the possible measured values, often only a subset of what classical mechanics allows.

concepts.name: The Schrödinger equation as an eigenvalue problem
concepts.statement: The time-independent Schrödinger equation Ĥψ = Eψ is an eigenvalue equation of the Hamiltonian whose eigenvalues are the allowed total energies.

concepts.name: Correspondence principle
concepts.statement: Bohr's principle that the behavior of systems described by quantum theory reproduces classical physics in the limit of large quantum numbers; the Hamiltonian follows from p²/2m + V by replacing p with −iħ d/dx.

concepts.name: Linear momentum operator
concepts.statement: The operator of the linear momentum of a particle moving along x, p̂ₓ = −iħ ∂/∂x, and −iħ∇ in three dimensions.

concepts.name: Position operator
concepts.statement: The operator of the position of a particle is multiplication by the coordinate: x̂ = x, and r̂ = r in three dimensions.

concepts.name: Kinetic energy operator
concepts.statement: The quantum counterpart of p²/2m: KÊ = −(ħ²/2m) ∂²/∂x², and −(ħ²/2m)∇² in three dimensions.

concepts.name: Angular momentum operator
concepts.statement: The cross product of the position and momentum operators, L̂ = −iħ(r × ∇).

concepts.name: Eigenstate
concepts.statement: A system whose wavefunction is an eigenfunction of an operator is in an eigenstate of that observable, and a measurement gives the eigenvalue; eigenstate and wavefunction are often used interchangeably.

concepts.name: A wavefunction as a superposition of eigenstates
concepts.statement: A wavefunction that is not an eigenstate of an operator can usually be written as a sum of its eigenstates, ψ = Σ cᵢφᵢ.

concepts.name: Collapse of the wavefunction
concepts.statement: A measurement leaves the wavefunction in an eigenstate of the measured observable, and only eigenvalues are observed: the wavefunction collapses into an eigenstate.

concepts.name: Square of the modulus
concepts.statement: The product of a wavefunction and its complex conjugate, Ψ*Ψ = |Ψ|², which is real.

concepts.name: Probability density
concepts.statement: The probability per unit volume of finding the particle at a point; in one dimension, per unit length.

concepts.name: Born interpretation
concepts.statement: Born proposed in 1926 that the square of the modulus of the wavefunction is the probability density of the particle: the wavefunction is a probability amplitude, and |ψ|² dτ the probability of finding the particle in the volume element dτ.

concepts.name: Volume element
concepts.statement: The element dτ a probability density is integrated over, written in the coordinates adopted: dx dy dz in Cartesian, r² sin φ dr dθ dφ in spherical, r dr dφ dz in cylindrical coordinates.

concepts.name: Probability of finding a particle in a region
concepts.statement: The probability that a measurement finds a particle between a and b is the integral of |ψ|² from a to b, the area under the probability density; in three dimensions the integral runs over the volume.

concepts.name: Well-behaved wavefunction
concepts.statement: A valid wavefunction is single-valued, finite and continuous everywhere; these conditions restrict the solutions of the Schrödinger equation so that only certain energies are allowed.

concepts.name: Particle in a box
concepts.statement: A particle free to move between two impenetrable walls, the simplest non-trivial application of the Schrödinger equation and one that can be solved exactly.

concepts.name: Potential of a one-dimensional box
concepts.statement: The potential energy is zero between x = 0 and x = L and infinite outside, so the particle cannot be found outside the box.

forms.latex: V(x)=\begin{cases} 0 & 0\leq x\leq L \\ \infty & x< 0 \; \text{and}\; x> L \end{cases}

concepts.name: Energy levels of a particle in a box
concepts.statement: The boundary conditions ψ(0) = ψ(L) = 0 allow only kL = nπ, so the energy of a particle in a box is quantized, Eₙ = h²n²/8mL² with n = 1, 2, 3, …

concepts.name: Ground state
concepts.statement: The state of lowest energy of a quantum system.

concepts.name: Zero-point energy
concepts.statement: The energy of the ground state in excess of the classical minimum; a particle in a box keeps E₁ = h²/8mL² > 0, and the motion with this energy is the zero-point motion.

concepts.name: Wavefunctions of a particle in a box
concepts.statement: The normalized eigenfunctions of a particle in a box are ψₙ(x) = √(2/L) sin(nπx/L), the same in form as the standing waves on a string.

concepts.name: Normalization condition
concepts.statement: A wavefunction is normalized when the integral of |ψ|² over all space is 1, since a measurement of the position must find the particle somewhere.

concepts.name: More nodes, higher energy
concepts.statement: The nth state of a particle in a box has n − 1 nodes; more nodes mean sharper curvature and a larger second derivative, so it is generally true that the energy of a quantum state rises with its number of nodes.

concepts.name: Orthogonality
concepts.statement: Two functions are orthogonal when the integral of the product of one's complex conjugate with the other over all space is zero.

concepts.name: Kronecker delta
concepts.statement: δₘₙ is 1 when m = n and 0 when m ≠ n.

concepts.name: Orthonormality
concepts.statement: A set of functions that are each normalized and orthogonal to one another, ∫ψₘψₙ dx = δₘₙ, is orthonormal.

concepts.name: The particle-in-a-box eigenfunctions are orthonormal
concepts.statement: The eigenfunctions of a particle in a box satisfy ∫₀ᴸ ψₘψₙ dx = δₘₙ; orthogonality follows from sin α sin β = ½[cos(α − β) − cos(α + β)].

concepts.name: Normalizing a wavefunction
concepts.statement: Multiplying a wavefunction by the constant that makes the integral of its square modulus over all space equal to 1.

concepts.name: Square-integrable wavefunction
concepts.statement: A wavefunction whose integral of |ψ|² over all space converges, so that it can be normalized; a plane wave is not square-integrable.

concepts.name: Normalization is kept in time
concepts.statement: A square-integrable wavefunction that is normalized at one instant stays normalized as it evolves by the time-dependent Schrödinger equation, since the boundary term vanishes as |x| → ∞.

concepts.name: Expectation value
concepts.statement: The probabilistic expected value of a measurement, the weighted average of all possible values, ⟨s⟩ = Σ s(i)Pₛ(i); it need not be a possible value itself.

concepts.name: Quantum expectation value
concepts.statement: The average of an observable o over many measurements on a state ψ is ⟨o⟩ = ∫ψ*Ôψ dx: the probability weights become |ψ|² and the scalar becomes the operator.

concepts.name: Average energy
concepts.statement: The average total energy ⟨H⟩ = ∫ψ*Ĥψ dx is the average kinetic energy plus the average potential energy.

concepts.name: Average position of a particle in a box
concepts.statement: The probability density of a particle in a box is symmetric about the center, so ⟨x⟩ = L/2.

concepts.name: Average momentum of a particle in a box
concepts.statement: The average momentum of a particle in a box is zero in every state, though its kinetic energy is not: it is equally likely to move in the +x and −x directions.

concepts.name: Momentum eigenfunctions
concepts.statement: e^{ikx} and e^{−ikx} are eigenfunctions of the momentum operator with eigenvalues +ħk and −ħk, waves moving right and left; the sine of a particle in a box is a combination of the two.

concepts.name: Uncertainty of an observable
concepts.statement: The uncertainty in a quantity A for a wavefunction is ΔA = √(⟨A²⟩ − ⟨A⟩²), from the expectation values of Â² and Â.

concepts.name: Particle in a three-dimensional box
concepts.statement: Separating ψ = X(x)Y(y)Z(z) turns the 3D box into three 1D boxes: ψ is a product of three sines and E = (h²/8m)(nₓ²/Lₓ² + n_y²/L_y² + n_z²/L_z²).

concepts.name: Degeneracy
concepts.statement: An energy level is degenerate when several different stationary states or wavefunctions have its energy, and non-degenerate when only one does.

concepts.name: Degree of degeneracy
concepts.statement: The number of independent wavefunctions for the stationary states of an energy level.

concepts.name: Degeneracy in a cube
concepts.statement: In a cube the energy depends only on nₓ² + n_y² + n_z², so states whose quantum numbers are permutations of one another share an energy: the first excited level is triply degenerate.

concepts.name: Accidental degeneracy
concepts.statement: A degeneracy that arises not from a symmetry such as Lₓ = L_y but from different combinations of nₓ²/Lₓ², n_y²/L_y² and n_z²/L_z² giving the same sum.

concepts.name: Classical state
concepts.statement: In classical mechanics the configuration or state of a system is a point (x, p) in the space of coordinates and momenta, which fixes every observable Q(x, p) in a fully deterministic way.

concepts.name: Postulate I: the wavefunction specifies the state
concepts.statement: The state of a system is completely specified by its wavefunction ψ(r, t), sometimes called the state function: all possible information about the system can be found in it.

concepts.name: A wavefunction has a first derivative
concepts.statement: Because the wavefunction must satisfy the Schrödinger equation, a second-order differential equation, its second derivative must exist, so its first derivative must exist too: a wavefunction with a break or a kink is not acceptable.

concepts.name: Postulate II: an operator for every observable
concepts.statement: For every observable property of a system there is a corresponding quantum mechanical operator: an observable written classically as Q(x, p) has the operator Q(x̂, p̂). The book calls this the Correspondence Principle.

concepts.name: Potential energy operator
concepts.statement: The potential energy operator V̂(x, y, z) multiplies the wavefunction by the potential energy V(x, y, z); with the kinetic energy operator it makes up the Hamiltonian, Ĥ = T̂ + V̂.

concepts.name: An eigenstate has no spread
concepts.statement: In an eigenstate ψ_a of Â the expectation value of A is the eigenvalue a and that of A² is a², so the variance of A is zero: every measurement of A in that state yields a.

concepts.name: Expectation value with an unnormalized wavefunction
concepts.statement: With a wavefunction that is not normalized, the expectation value of an observable is ∫ψ*Âψ dx divided by the normalization integral ∫ψ*ψ dx.

concepts.name: Variance
concepts.statement: The variance of x, σ²ₓ = ∫(x − ⟨x⟩)²|ψ|² dx = ⟨x²⟩ − ⟨x⟩², measures how far the results of many measurements of x scatter around the expectation value ⟨x⟩; its square root σₓ is the standard deviation.

concepts.name: Completeness of eigenstates
concepts.statement: The eigenstates of an operator attributed to an observable form a complete set: any general wavefunction can be written as a linear combination of them, ψ = Σ cᵢφᵢ, with complex weights cᵢ.

concepts.name: Expansion coefficients
concepts.statement: The weight of an eigenstate φᵢ in the expansion of a wavefunction ψ is the overlap cᵢ = ∫φᵢ*ψ dx, because the eigenstates are orthonormal.

concepts.name: The squared expansion coefficients sum to one
concepts.statement: For a properly normalized wavefunction the squared moduli of its expansion coefficients add up to one, Σ|cᵢ|² = 1.

concepts.name: A stationary state's probability density is constant
concepts.statement: A system prepared in an eigenstate ψₙ of the Hamiltonian evolves as Ψ(x,t) = ψₙ(x)e^{−iEₙt/ħ}, which satisfies the time-dependent Schrödinger equation; its probability density |Ψ(x,t)|² = |ψₙ(x)|² does not change in time, and its energy stays fixed at Eₙ.

concepts.name: Nonstationary state
concepts.statement: A linear combination of eigenstates of different energies, such as Ψ(x,0) = [ψ₁(x) + ψ₂(x)]/√2, is not a stationary state: its probability density changes with time.

concepts.name: Observer effect
concepts.statement: Measuring a quantum system changes how it evolves in time, so the experimenter is coupled to the system and the act of observing influences the phenomenon observed; a classical system evolves by Newton's laws whether or not it is observed.

concepts.name: Eigenvalues of observables are real
concepts.statement: The eigenvalues of operators associated with experimental measurements are all real, a* = a, since they are the values measured.

concepts.name: Orthogonality theorem
concepts.statement: Eigenfunctions of a Hermitian operator are orthogonal if they have different eigenvalues: nondegenerate eigenfunctions of the same operator are orthogonal.

concepts.name: Overlap integral
concepts.statement: The overlap integral of two normalized functions, S = ∫ψₐ*ψₐ′ dx, measures how far they fail to be orthogonal: it is zero for orthogonal functions.

concepts.name: Orthogonalizing degenerate eigenfunctions
concepts.statement: Degenerate eigenfunctions are not automatically orthogonal, but can be made so by the Gram–Schmidt orthogonalization: subtracting from ψₐ′ its overlap with ψₐ, ψₐ″ = ψₐ′ − Sψₐ, gives an eigenfunction of the same eigenvalue orthogonal to ψₐ.

concepts.name: Eigenstates can be chosen orthogonal
concepts.statement: The eigenstates of a Hermitian operator are, or can be chosen to be, mutually orthogonal: those of different eigenvalues are orthogonal already, and degenerate ones can be combined into orthogonal ones.

concepts.name: Commuting operators share eigenfunctions
concepts.statement: If two operators commute, ÂB̂ = B̂Â, they can have the same set of eigenfunctions, and the corresponding physical quantities can be measured exactly simultaneously, with no limit on the uncertainty.

concepts.name: General Heisenberg uncertainty principle
concepts.statement: If two operators do not commute, the standard deviations of their quantities in any state are bounded below by the expectation value of their commutator, so neither can be zero unless the other is infinite; if they commute, there is no restriction.

concepts.name: Commutation of angular momentum
concepts.statement: The square of the angular momentum commutes with each of its components, but the components do not commute with one another, so the magnitude of the angular momentum and one component (usually z) can be known at the same time while nothing is known about the other components.

concepts.name: Translation, rotation and vibration of a diatomic molecule
concepts.statement: The motion of the two atoms of a diatomic molecule separates into the translation of its center of mass and two internal motions that leave the center of mass where it is: rotation, modeled by the rigid rotor, and vibration, modeled by the harmonic oscillator.

concepts.name: Harmonic oscillator
concepts.statement: The model of a mass held by a restoring force proportional to its displacement, F = −kx, which the book uses for the vibration of a diatomic molecule.

concepts.name: Rigid rotor
concepts.statement: The model of a rotating system of two point masses held at fixed distances from their center of mass, which the book uses for the rotation of a diatomic molecule when its vibration is ignored.

concepts.name: Hooke's law
concepts.statement: The restoring force on a mass displaced from its equilibrium position is proportional to the displacement and opposite to it: F = −kx.

concepts.name: Force constant
concepts.statement: The constant k of Hooke's law, which reflects the stiffness of a spring or a bond: the larger it is, the stiffer the spring or the bond. It is the second derivative of the potential energy at its minimum.

concepts.name: Vibrational coordinate
concepts.statement: The change in the bond length from the equilibrium bond length, the displacement x along which a diatomic molecule vibrates.

concepts.name: Harmonic potential
concepts.statement: The potential energy of a Hooke's-law system increases quadratically with the displacement, V = ½kx², and minus its first derivative is the Hooke's-law force.

concepts.name: Equation of motion of the harmonic oscillator
concepts.statement: Newton's second law with the Hooke's-law force gives the classical equation of motion m d²x/dt² = −kx, a linear second-order differential equation.

concepts.name: Harmonic motion
concepts.statement: The solution of the classical oscillator's equation of motion is a sinusoidal displacement x(t) = x₀ sin(ωt + φ), with momentum p = mx₀ω cos(ωt + φ); such motion is called harmonic.

concepts.name: Frequency of a harmonic oscillator
concepts.statement: The angular frequency of a harmonic oscillator, ω = √(k/m), depends only on its force constant and its mass (the reduced mass μ for a molecule), not on its energy: a stiffer spring vibrates faster and a heavier mass slower.

concepts.name: Energy of the classical harmonic oscillator
concepts.statement: The energy of the oscillator is the sum of its kinetic and potential energies, E = p²/2m + kx²/2; it is shifted continuously between the two and equals ½kA², the potential energy at the turning points, so it changes continuously with the amplitude.

concepts.name: Turning points
concepts.statement: The displacements x = ±A at which all the oscillator's energy is potential energy, so it stops and reverses; a classical oscillator can never be found beyond them.

concepts.name: Where a classical oscillator is found
concepts.statement: A classical oscillator spends the longest time near its turning points, where it slows down and reverses, so the probability of finding it is highest there and lowest at the equilibrium position; its lowest energy is zero, at rest at the bottom of the well.

concepts.name: Reduced mass
concepts.statement: The mass μ = m_A m_B/(m_A + m_B) of the single particle that represents a two-body system whose bodies move only under their mutual interaction, so the vibration and rotation separate from the motion of the center of mass.

concepts.name: Schrödinger equation of the harmonic oscillator
concepts.statement: With the quadratic potential ½kx² and the reduced mass μ, the Schrödinger equation of the quantum harmonic oscillator is [−(ħ²/2μ) d²/dx² + ½kx²]ψ = Eψ.

concepts.name: Vibrational quantum number
concepts.statement: The quantum number v = 0, 1, 2, … that labels the harmonic oscillator's energy levels; it is a Latin v, not the Greek ν of the frequency.

concepts.name: Energy levels of the harmonic oscillator
concepts.statement: The energies of the quantum harmonic oscillator are quantized, E_v = (v + ½)hν = (v + ½)ħω with v = 0, 1, 2, …: equally spaced by hν, the lowest above the bottom of the potential.

concepts.name: Isotope effect
concepts.statement: Substituting one isotope for another changes the reduced mass and so the vibrational frequency while the force constant stays nearly the same; vibrational frequencies need the masses of specific isotopes, not the atomic weights of the periodic table.

concepts.name: Taylor expansion of a potential
concepts.statement: Any potential near a stable equilibrium x₀ can be expanded as a Taylor series in x − x₀; with V(x₀) = 0 and no linear term at the minimum, it starts with the harmonic term ½kx², and the cubic term γx³/6 is the first anharmonic correction.

concepts.name: Anharmonicity
concepts.statement: The deviation of a system from harmonic oscillation: the restoring force is no longer proportional to the displacement and the potential is not strictly quadratic.

concepts.name: Anharmonic vibrational levels
concepts.statement: A real vibrational potential has levels E_v = (v + ½)ν_e − (v + ½)²ν_e x_e + (v + ½)³ν_e y_e + …, with anharmonicity constants x_e and y_e; they become less widely spaced at high excitation because the potential is less confining than a parabola.

concepts.name: Well depth
concepts.statement: The depth D_e of a molecule's potential, measured from its minimum to the dissociation limit; it is larger than the dissociation energy D₀ by the zero-point energy.

concepts.name: Dissociation energy
concepts.statement: The energy D₀ needed to break the bond, measured from the lowest (v = 0) vibrational level to the dissociation limit.

concepts.name: Limitations of the harmonic oscillator model
concepts.statement: Because its levels are equally spaced, the harmonic oscillator predicts a single-line vibrational spectrum where many lines (overtones) are seen, and it cannot dissociate however much energy it is given.

concepts.name: Morse potential
concepts.statement: The potential V(x) = D(1 − e^{−β(x − x₀)})², which includes bond breaking and the anharmonicity of real bonds: zero at the equilibrium separation and D at infinite separation, its levels crowding together toward the dissociation energy.

concepts.name: Zero-point energy of the harmonic oscillator
concepts.statement: The lowest energy of the quantum oscillator is E₀ = ħω/2, not zero, so the atoms of a molecule are moving even in the lowest vibrational state, in direct contrast to the classical oscillator at rest.

concepts.name: Classical limit of the displacement
concepts.statement: Equating the zero-point energy to the potential energy at maximum extension gives the classical limit Q₀ of the oscillator's displacement: ħω/2 = kQ₀²/2.

concepts.name: Average displacement and momentum of the oscillator
concepts.statement: Because the potential is symmetric about Q = 0, a displacement Q > 0 is as likely as Q < 0, so the average displacement ⟨Q⟩ and the average momentum ⟨P_Q⟩ are zero, though the oscillator is not sitting still.

concepts.name: Root-mean-square displacement
concepts.statement: The standard deviation of the displacement (and, likewise, the root-mean-square momentum), used as the measure of the uncertainty in the oscillator's position and momentum, since their averages are zero.

concepts.name: Orthonormality of the oscillator wavefunctions
concepts.statement: The harmonic oscillator wavefunctions form an orthonormal set: each is normalized and any two with different v are orthogonal.

concepts.name: Classically forbidden region
concepts.statement: The region beyond the classical limits of the displacement, where the potential energy would exceed the total energy; the quantum oscillator's wavefunctions extend into it.

concepts.name: Infrared spectroscopy
concepts.statement: The study of the absorption of infrared radiation (about 4000 to 40 cm⁻¹) by transitions between vibrational levels, used to identify functional groups and compounds by their characteristic, fingerprint spectra.

concepts.name: Frequency of a vibrational transition
concepts.statement: A photon is absorbed or emitted when its energy matches the difference between two vibrational levels, hν_photon = (v′ − v)hν_m; for adjacent levels its frequency is identical to the classical vibrational frequency of the bond, (1/2π)√(k/μ), or (1/2πc)√(k/μ) in wavenumbers.

concepts.name: Selection rule
concepts.statement: A rule that limits which transitions between states are allowed and so observed in a spectrum.

concepts.name: Dipole moment
concepts.statement: The dipole moment of a molecule, the sum of each particle's charge times its position; μ_{x=0} is its value with the nuclei at their equilibrium positions.

concepts.name: Dipole moment operator
concepts.statement: The operator μ̂ = Σ e r⃗ + Σ q R⃗ summed over all the electrons and nuclei of the molecule, each charge times its position vector.

concepts.name: Transition moment integral
concepts.statement: The integral μ_T = ⟨ψ_v′|μ̂|ψ_v⟩ that expresses the probability of a transition between two states: where it is zero the transition is forbidden.

concepts.name: Forbidden transition
concepts.statement: A transition whose transition moment integral is zero, so it is not observed; transitions with low probabilities are weakly allowed and those with high probabilities strongly allowed.

concepts.name: Selection rules for IR absorption
concepts.statement: A vibration absorbs infrared radiation only if it changes the molecule's dipole moment, dμ/dx ≠ 0, and only between adjacent levels, Δv = ±1; so the harmonic oscillator's IR spectrum is a single line at ħω, and symmetric molecules such as O₂ and N₂ do not absorb.

concepts.name: Overtone transition
concepts.statement: A transition with Δv = ±n, n > 1, forbidden in the harmonic oscillator model and seen because molecular vibrations are anharmonic; the first overtone, Δv = 2, appears at slightly less than twice the frequency of the fundamental, Δv = 1.

concepts.name: Harmonic oscillator equation in a scaled coordinate
concepts.statement: Collecting constants in β² = ħ/√(μk) and changing the variable to x = q/β turns the oscillator's Schrödinger equation into d²ψ/dx² + (2μβ²E/ħ² − x²)ψ = 0.

concepts.name: Solving by an asymptotic form times a power series
concepts.statement: Find a solution valid for large values of the variable, then write the complete solution as that asymptotic solution times a power series, truncated to give a family of solutions.

concepts.name: Hermite polynomials
concepts.statement: The polynomials H_v(x) of degree v (H₀ = 1, H₁ = 2x, H₂ = 4x² − 2, …), standard functions from the work of Charles Hermite, that solve the harmonic oscillator equation when multiplied by e^{−x²/2}.

concepts.name: Harmonic oscillator wavefunctions
concepts.statement: The harmonic oscillator wavefunctions are ψ_v(x) = N_v H_v(x) e^{−x²/2} with N_v = 1/(2^v v! √π)^{1/2}: a Hermite polynomial times a Gaussian that falls off at large displacement.

concepts.name: Nodes and symmetry of the oscillator wavefunctions
concepts.statement: The wavefunction ψ_v has v nodes, and its symmetry alternates: gerade (even) for even v, ungerade (odd) for odd v.

concepts.name: Quantum mechanical tunneling
concepts.statement: A quantum oscillator has a finite probability of being in a region where its potential energy exceeds its total energy, beyond the classical limits, so the amplitude of a molecular vibration is larger than the classical picture allows.

concepts.name: Error function
concepts.statement: The integral (2/√π)∫₀^z e^{−x²}dx, which can only be evaluated numerically; ERF(1) = 0.843.

concepts.name: Probability of the forbidden region in the ground state
concepts.statement: For v = 0, P[allowed] = (2/√π)∫₀¹ e^{−x²}dx = ERF(1) = 0.843, so the oscillator is found beyond its classical limits 16% of the time.

concepts.name: Even function
concepts.statement: A function with f(−x) = f(x) for all x, symmetric about the y axis, such as x² and cos x.

concepts.name: Odd function
concepts.statement: A function with f(−x) = −f(x) for all x, unchanged by a rotation of 180° about the origin, such as x³ and sin x.

concepts.name: Products of even and odd functions
concepts.statement: The product of two even functions or of two odd functions is even; the product of an even and an odd function is odd.

concepts.name: Integrals of even and odd functions
concepts.statement: Over an interval symmetric about zero, the integral of an even function is twice the integral over half the interval and the integral of an odd function is zero, whatever the function.

concepts.name: Hermite recurrence relation
concepts.statement: Each Hermite polynomial can be generated from the two before it: H_{n+1}(x) = 2xH_n(x) − 2nH_{n−1}(x).

concepts.name: Parity of the Hermite polynomials
concepts.statement: H_n(−x) = (−1)ⁿH_n(x): a Hermite polynomial is even when n is even and odd when n is odd.

concepts.name: Orthogonality of the Hermite polynomials
concepts.statement: The Hermite polynomials are orthogonal with the weight function e^{−x²}: ∫H_mH_n e^{−x²}dx is zero for m ≠ n and 2ⁿn!√π for m = n, the integral that normalizes the oscillator wavefunctions.

concepts.name: Angular velocity
concepts.statement: The rate of rotation ω = v/r of a particle moving at speed v at a distance r from the axis.

concepts.name: Angular momentum
concepts.statement: The rotational counterpart of linear momentum: for a rigid body rotating with angular velocity ω about an axis, L = Iω, the sum of the angular momenta of its particles.

concepts.name: Moment of inertia
concepts.statement: The inertial resistance of a body to rotation about an axis; for a diatomic rigid rotor about its center of mass it is I = μr₀².

concepts.name: Kinetic energy of a rotating body
concepts.statement: The energy of a classical rigid rotor is all kinetic, T = ½Iω² = L²/2I, and grows with the rate of rotation and the moment of inertia; it is not quantized.

concepts.name: Spherical coordinates
concepts.statement: Coordinates that place a point by its distance r from the origin, its polar angle θ from the z axis and its azimuthal angle φ from the x axis; for a rigid rotor r is fixed and only θ and φ vary, on the surface of a sphere of radius r₀.

concepts.name: Schrödinger equation of the rigid rotor
concepts.statement: With r fixed at r₀ and I = μr₀², the rigid rotor's Schrödinger equation contains only the angles: −(ħ²/2I)[(1/sin θ)∂/∂θ(sin θ ∂/∂θ) + (1/sin²θ)∂²/∂φ²]ΘΦ = EΘΦ.

concepts.name: The θ and φ equations of the rigid rotor
concepts.statement: Writing the wavefunction as Θ(θ)Φ(φ) and setting both sides of the separated equation equal to the constant m_J² gives a θ-equation and a φ-equation, d²Φ/dφ² + m_J²Φ = 0, each in one variable.

concepts.name: Cyclic boundary condition
concepts.statement: Because φ and φ + 2π are the same point in space, the wavefunction must repeat around the circle: Φ(φ) = Φ(φ + 2π).

concepts.name: The φ functions of the rigid rotor
concepts.statement: The φ-equation's normalized solutions are Φ(φ) = (1/√2π)e^{±im_Jφ}, and the cyclic boundary condition requires m_J = 0, ±1, ±2, ….

concepts.name: Associated Legendre functions
concepts.statement: The power series of sine and cosine functions that solve the rigid rotor's θ-equation, giving the Θ(θ) functions.

concepts.name: Rigid rotor quantum numbers
concepts.statement: The two quantum numbers of the rigid rotor: J = 0, 1, 2, …, which fixes the length of the angular momentum vector and the energy, and m_J, which fixes its component along z and ranges over −J, …, J.

concepts.name: Energy levels of the rigid rotor
concepts.statement: Solving the θ-equation requires λ = J(J + 1), so the rotor's energy is quantized, E = J(J + 1)ħ²/2I, depending only on J; the spacing between levels increases as J increases.

concepts.name: Degeneracy of the rotor levels
concepts.statement: Each energy level of the rigid rotor is (2J + 1)-fold degenerate, since m_J runs from +J to −J in integer steps: the energy does not depend on the orientation of the rotor.

concepts.name: Spherical harmonics
concepts.statement: The rigid rotor wavefunctions Y^{m_J}_J(θ, φ) = Θ^{|m_J|}_J(θ)Φ_{m_J}(φ), labeled by both quantum numbers; their squares have the shapes of the s, p and d orbitals.

concepts.name: Probability of a rotor's orientation
concepts.statement: The probability of finding the internuclear axis at θ₀, φ₀ within the area element ds = sin θ dθ dφ is Y*Y ds: the absolute square of the spherical harmonic is the probability density over orientations.

concepts.name: A quantum rotor does not rotate classically
concepts.statement: In the J = 1, m_J = 0 state the whole xy-plane is a node, so the internuclear axis is never found there, though a classical molecule rotating through it would lie in it twice a revolution: molecules are not rotating in the classical sense, but keep the properties of angular momentum.

concepts.name: Rotations of a molecule
concepts.statement: An object has three orthogonal rotations, about the x, y and z axes; for a linear molecule the motion about the internuclear axis is not counted as a rotation.

concepts.name: Microwave spectroscopy
concepts.statement: The permanent dipole moment of a polar molecule couples to radiation and induces transitions between rotational states, whose energies fall in the far infrared and microwave regions.

concepts.name: Rotational selection rules
concepts.statement: The transition moment integral of the spherical harmonics allows rotational transitions only with ΔJ = ±1 and Δm_J = 0, ±1, and only in molecules with a permanent dipole moment; a photon is absorbed for ΔJ = +1 and emitted for ΔJ = −1.

concepts.name: Rotational constant
concepts.statement: The constant B = ħ²/2I of a molecule's rotational levels, written in frequency as B/h = h/(8π²μr₀²) and in wavenumbers as B̃ = B/hc; it depends on the bond length and the reduced mass.

concepts.name: Rotational transition energies
concepts.statement: With J_f = J_i + 1, the energy of the photon absorbed in a rotational transition is E_photon = hν = 2B(J_i + 1): the first line lies at 2B, the next at 4B.

concepts.name: Spacing of rotational lines
concepts.statement: The rigid rotor predicts a rotational spectrum of exactly equally spaced lines, 2B apart.

concepts.name: Centrifugal stretching
concepts.statement: As the rotational angular momentum increases with J the bond stretches, increasing the moment of inertia and decreasing the rotational constant, so the observed lines draw slightly closer: a molecule is not really a rigid rotor.

concepts.name: Finding a bond length from a rotational spectrum
concepts.statement: Read the J = 0 → 1 line (or the line spacing) as 2B, compute the reduced mass from the isotopes' masses, and solve B = h/(8π²μr₀²) for the bond length.

concepts.name: Observable
concepts.statement: A physical observable is anything about a system that can be measured, such as position, momentum or energy; quantum mechanics has an operator for every observable.

concepts.name: Hydrogen atom as a reduced particle
concepts.statement: The internal motion of the electron and proton about their center of mass is that of one particle of reduced mass μ at the position r of the electron relative to the proton; since the proton is so much heavier, the chapter takes μ as the electron mass and puts the proton at the center of mass.

concepts.name: Central potential
concepts.statement: A potential energy that depends only on the distance r from a center and on no angle, as the Coulomb attraction between the electron and the proton does.

concepts.name: Schrödinger equation of the hydrogen atom
concepts.statement: The time-independent Schrödinger equation of the hydrogen atom uses the kinetic energy operator of the rigid rotor in spherical coordinates, with r now free to vary, and the Coulomb potential energy −e²/4πε₀r of the electron and proton.

concepts.name: Square of the angular momentum operator
concepts.statement: The operator for the square of the angular momentum, the angular part of the Laplacian times −ħ²; the book writes it M̂² and, for an electron, L̂². It is also the sum of the squares of the three component operators.

concepts.name: Separating the radial and angular motion
concepts.statement: Because L̂² does not involve r, a product ψ = R(r)Y(θ, φ) separates the hydrogen atom's equation into a radial differential equation and an angular one, each equal to the same constant λ.

concepts.name: Eigenvalues of the square of the angular momentum
concepts.statement: The spherical harmonics are the eigenfunctions of L̂², with eigenvalue l(l + 1)ħ², the rigid rotor's J(J + 1)ħ² in the notation for electrons.

concepts.name: Radial equation of the hydrogen atom
concepts.statement: With λ = l(l + 1)ħ², the radial part of the hydrogen atom's equation is an equation for R(r) alone, in which the angular momentum enters as the term l(l + 1)ħ²/2μr² beside the potential energy.

concepts.name: Radial function
concepts.statement: The factor R(r) of a hydrogen atom wavefunction, a solution of the radial equation, which describes how far the electron is from the proton.

concepts.name: Hydrogen atom wavefunctions
concepts.statement: The solutions of the hydrogen atom's Schrödinger equation are products of a radial function and a spherical harmonic, labelled by three quantum numbers n, l and m_l; |ψ|² dτ is the probability of finding the electron in the volume element dτ at r, θ, φ.

concepts.name: Principal quantum number
concepts.statement: The quantum number n = 1, 2, 3, … of the hydrogen atom, which fixes its energy.

concepts.name: Angular momentum quantum number
concepts.statement: The quantum number l of the hydrogen atom, which fixes the magnitude of the electron's angular momentum; it is also called the azimuthal or orbital quantum number.

concepts.name: Magnetic quantum number
concepts.statement: The quantum number m_l of the hydrogen atom, which fixes the z component of the angular momentum; it is named for the dependence of the energy on m_l in a magnetic field.

concepts.name: Allowed values of n, l and m_l
concepts.statement: The boundary conditions allow n = 1, 2, 3, …; l = 0 to n − 1; and 2l + 1 values of m_l from −l to +l in integer steps.

concepts.name: Degeneracy of the hydrogen levels
concepts.statement: The number of orbitals with a given n, all of one energy, is n².

concepts.name: Orbital letters s, p, d, f
concepts.statement: The letters that code the value of l: s for 0, p for 1, d for 2, f for 3, then alphabetically from g; they come from early spectroscopy (sharp, principal, diffuse, fundamental).

concepts.name: Atomic orbital
concepts.statement: A function that describes one electron in an atom; the hydrogen atom wavefunctions are its atomic orbitals, and an electron described by one is said to be in it. An orbital is not an orbit: it gives no trajectory.

concepts.name: Real orbitals from complex ones
concepts.statement: Since any combination of degenerate solutions is a solution, the complex wavefunctions with m_l = ±1 (and ±2) can be combined into real ones such as p_x and p_y; only m_l = 0 belongs to one real orbital (p_z, d_z²) by itself.

concepts.name: Picturing an orbital
concepts.statement: An orbital's density is a function of three variables, pictured by shading small volume elements in proportion to ψ*ψ, by contour maps in a plane, or by plotting the radial and angular parts separately.

concepts.name: Radial node
concepts.statement: A value of r, other than 0 or ∞, at which the radial function is zero.

concepts.name: Number of radial nodes
concepts.statement: A hydrogen wavefunction has n − l − 1 radial nodes: none for 1s, one for 2s, and so on; the roots of its Laguerre polynomial are its radial nodes.

concepts.name: Only s orbitals are nonzero at the nucleus
concepts.statement: Every s function has a nonzero value at r = 0, while p, d, f and all other functions go to zero at the origin.

concepts.name: Radial probability density
concepts.statement: The square R(r)*R(r) of the radial function, the density of the electron at a point a distance r from the proton.

concepts.name: Radial distribution function
concepts.statement: The probability density of finding the electron anywhere on the sphere of radius r: the density on that sphere times its area 4πr², which for a normalized radial function is r²R(r)² (the book writes 4πr²R*R, which counts the 4π twice). It is zero at r = 0, rises with the r² term and falls once the exponential decay wins.

concepts.name: Orbital angular momentum
concepts.statement: The angular momentum of a particle about the origin, the cross product of its position and its momentum, with components L_x, L_y and L_z; for a circular orbit its magnitude is mvr.

concepts.name: Operators for the components of angular momentum
concepts.statement: The operators L̂_x, L̂_y and L̂_z, written from the classical components with the position and momentum operators; in spherical coordinates L̂_z = −iħ ∂/∂φ.

concepts.name: Magnitude of the angular momentum
concepts.statement: The square of the angular momentum can take only the values l(l + 1)ħ², so its magnitude is √(l(l + 1)) ħ, with l = 0, 1, 2, …; a state of quantum number l is often said to have angular momentum l for short.

concepts.name: Quantized z component of angular momentum
concepts.statement: The z component of the angular momentum can take only the values m_l ħ, with m_l an integer from −l to l.

concepts.name: Commutation relations of angular momentum
concepts.statement: The components of orbital angular momentum do not commute: [L̂_x, L̂_y] = iħL̂_z and its cyclic permutations. Any three operators that satisfy these relations represent the components of some sort of angular momentum.

concepts.name: Vector model of angular momentum
concepts.statement: A state with quantum numbers l and m_l is drawn as a vector of length √(l(l + 1)) ħ whose z component is m_l ħ; since L_x and L_y cannot be known with L_z, every such vector, on a cone about z, represents it equally.

concepts.name: Radial function far from the nucleus
concepts.statement: Far from the nucleus the radial function decays as an exponential in r/na₀, like the harmonic oscillator's Gaussian tail but with r in place of r².

concepts.name: Associated Laguerre polynomials
concepts.statement: The polynomials L_{n,l}(r), from the truncated power series of the radial equation, labelled by n and l; acceptable solutions need n ≥ l + 1.

concepts.name: Hydrogen radial functions
concepts.statement: The radial functions are products of a normalization constant, (r/a₀)^l, an associated Laguerre polynomial and the decaying exponential, which overpowers the polynomial so that R(r) goes to zero at large r. With the nuclear charge Z they serve every one-electron atom or ion.

concepts.name: Energy levels of the hydrogen atom
concepts.statement: The condition n ≥ l + 1 quantizes the energy, giving the same levels as the Bohr model: E_n = −μe⁴/8ε₀²h²n², which depend on n alone.

concepts.name: Bohr and Schrödinger models compared
concepts.statement: The Schrödinger model gives no orbits, only probabilities; its angular momentum is √(l(l + 1)) ħ, which can be zero, where Bohr's is a whole number of ħ; and its quantum numbers arise from solving the equation, where Bohr postulated them.

concepts.name: Electron density distribution
concepts.statement: The probability distribution P_n of an electron in a definite energy level, read as the fraction of its charge in each small volume of space; it is measured in electronic charges per unit volume, e⁻/a₀³ in atomic units.

concepts.name: s orbitals are spherically symmetric
concepts.statement: For every n one orbital, the s orbital, is independent of direction: its density depends on r alone, so its contours in a plane through the nucleus are circles; the other n² − 1 are concentrated in planes or along axes.

concepts.name: Volume of a thin spherical shell
concepts.statement: The volume between spheres of radius r and r + Δr is 4πr²Δr when Δr is small, since the terms in Δr² and Δr³ become negligible.

concepts.name: Most probable radius of the 1s electron
concepts.statement: The radial distribution function of the hydrogen ground state is zero at the nucleus, rises to a maximum at r_max = a₀ and falls off; since the curve is unsymmetrical, the average r̄ lies beyond r_max.

concepts.name: Torque
concepts.statement: What changes a system's angular momentum, as a force changes its linear momentum.

concepts.name: A central force leaves angular momentum constant
concepts.statement: A force directed along r, like the attraction of the nucleus, changes only the electron's linear momentum: it exerts no torque, so the angular momentum of the orbit stays constant.

concepts.name: Conserved quantities are quantized
concepts.statement: The book's rule of thumb: any quantity that is constant in a classical system is conserved and quantized in the quantum system, so an undisturbed atom has quantized energy and angular momentum.

concepts.name: s orbitals carry no angular momentum
concepts.statement: When l = 0 the angular momentum is zero; only such s electrons have spherical density distributions and place density at the nucleus.

concepts.name: Number of nodes
concepts.statement: The number of nodes of a hydrogen orbital grows with its energy and equals n − 1, while the average r grows with n.

concepts.name: Shape of a p orbital
concepts.statement: A p orbital (l = 1) is concentrated along an axis: positive on one side of the nodal plane through the nucleus and negative on the other, with two lobes of circular cross section and no density at the nucleus.

concepts.name: Shape of a d orbital
concepts.statement: A d orbital (l = 2) has two angular nodes and no density at the nucleus; only d_z² belongs to one value of m_l (0), the others being combinations.

concepts.name: Zeeman effect
concepts.statement: The shift of an orbital's energy in an external magnetic field, which depends on m_l; with no field the 2l + 1 values of m_l have the same energy.

concepts.name: Electron–electron repulsion
concepts.statement: The Coulomb potential energy e²/4πε₀r_ij of two electrons a distance r_ij apart, positive because like charges repel.

concepts.name: Hamiltonian of a multi-electron atom
concepts.statement: The Hamiltonian of an atom with nuclear charge Z and n electrons, nucleus fixed at the center of mass, has a kinetic energy term and an attraction to the nucleus for each electron, and a repulsion term for each pair of electrons.

concepts.name: Multi-electron atoms cannot be solved exactly
concepts.statement: The repulsion terms in 1/r_ij depend on two electrons' coordinates at once, so the Hamiltonian does not separate electron by electron and the Schrödinger equation has no exact solution even for helium.

concepts.name: Multi-electron wavefunction
concepts.statement: A single function of the coordinates of all the electrons at once, whose square gives the probability of finding the electrons, though not particular ones, in a region.

concepts.name: Orbital approximation
concepts.statement: Writing a multi-electron wavefunction as a product of one-electron functions, the orbitals, so that the energy is approximately the sum of the one-electron energies.

concepts.name: Ionization energy
concepts.statement: The minimum energy needed to remove an electron from an atom or ion in the gas phase: the first ionization energy I₁ takes the first electron, and the second, I₂, takes the next one from the ion left behind.

concepts.name: Ground-state energy of helium
concepts.statement: Since the three separated particles have zero energy, helium's ground-state energy is minus the sum of its two ionization energies, −79.02 eV, or −5.8066 R_H; the second ionization energy follows exactly from the hydrogen-like ion He⁺.

concepts.name: Ignoring electron–electron repulsion
concepts.statement: Dropping the repulsion term e²/4πε₀r₁₂ leaves helium's Hamiltonian a sum of two hydrogen-like one-electron Hamiltonians, so the two electrons separate.

concepts.name: Additive one-electron energies
concepts.statement: When the Hamiltonian is a sum of one-electron Hamiltonians, the wavefunction is a product of one-electron wavefunctions and the energy is the sum of their energies; for helium with both electrons in 1s it gives −8R_H = −108.8 eV, far below the true −79.0 eV.

concepts.name: Shielding
concepts.statement: One electron's negative charge partly cancels the nucleus's attraction for another electron, so that electron feels a smaller nuclear charge than the nucleus carries.

concepts.name: Effective nuclear charge
concepts.statement: The reduced nuclear charge an electron feels once shielding is counted, written Z_eff or ζ; in helium it lies between 1, for complete shielding, and 2, for none.

concepts.name: Trial wavefunction
concepts.statement: An approximate wavefunction written with one or more adjustable parameters, which the variational method varies to lower its energy.

concepts.name: Variational energy
concepts.statement: The expectation value of the exact Hamiltonian in a trial wavefunction, divided by the trial function's normalization integral.

concepts.name: Variational principle
concepts.statement: For a time-independent Hamiltonian, the variational energy of any trial wavefunction is greater than or equal to the true ground-state energy, and equal to it only when the trial function is the true ground-state wavefunction; the variational energy is an upper bound.

concepts.name: Applying the variational method
concepts.statement: Define the Hamiltonian, choose a trial wavefunction with adjustable parameters, evaluate its variational energy as a function of them, and find the minimum by setting each derivative to zero; the minimum is the best estimate of the ground-state energy and fixes the best parameters.

concepts.name: Variational energy of helium
concepts.statement: With a product of two 1s functions of effective charge ζ as trial function and the complete helium Hamiltonian, the variational energy is E_h(ζ² − 27ζ/8); it is lowest at ζ = 27/16 ≈ 1.69, giving −77.5 eV, about 2% above the experimental −79.0 eV.

concepts.name: Basis functions
concepts.statement: The fixed functions combined in a linear trial wavefunction, chosen to obey the boundary conditions of the exact state, to depend on the same coordinates, to share its symmetry and to make the Hamiltonian's matrix elements easy to evaluate; they need not be orthogonal or normalized.

concepts.name: Linear variation function
concepts.statement: A trial wavefunction written as a linear combination of N linearly independent basis functions, whose coefficients a_j are the parameters varied.

concepts.name: Hamiltonian matrix element
concepts.statement: The integral of the Hamiltonian between two basis functions, H_ij = ⟨φ_i|Ĥ|φ_j⟩.

concepts.name: Variational energy of a linear trial function
concepts.statement: With a linear trial function the variational energy is a ratio of two sums over pairs of basis functions, one of Hamiltonian matrix elements and one of overlap integrals, and depends quadratically on the coefficients.

concepts.name: Secular equations
concepts.statement: Setting the derivative of the linear variational energy with respect to each coefficient to zero gives one linear equation for each k, Σ_i a_i(H_ik − E S_ik) = 0; with an orthonormal basis they become the matrix eigenvalue equation Σ_j H_ij a_j = E a_i.

concepts.name: Determinant
concepts.statement: A number computed from a square matrix: ad − bc for a 2 × 2 matrix, and for a larger one an expansion in minors and cofactors; a matrix has an inverse only when its determinant is not zero.

concepts.name: Secular determinant
concepts.statement: The secular equations have a solution other than all coefficients zero only when the determinant of H_ik − E S_ik vanishes; its roots, in order, approximate the energies of the lowest states, each lying above the true energy of its state.

concepts.name: Characteristic equation
concepts.statement: The polynomial in the energy obtained by expanding the secular determinant and setting it to zero, solved directly by linear algebra or numerically.

concepts.name: Bracketing theorem
concepts.statement: Between successive pairs of the eigenvalues found by solving the secular problem at least one exact eigenvalue lies.

concepts.name: Applying the linear variational method
concepts.statement: Write the trial function as a linear combination of basis functions, evaluate the H_ij and S_ij, solve the secular determinant for the energies, put each energy back into the secular equations for its coefficients and normalize; a larger basis gives more states.

concepts.name: Linear combination of atomic orbitals
concepts.statement: The linear variational method with atomic orbitals as the basis functions, used to compute the energies and wavefunctions of atoms and molecules.

concepts.name: Slater-type orbital
concepts.statement: A basis function made of a spherical harmonic times a hydrogen-like exponential decay e^{−αr}; it gives exact results for hydrogen.

concepts.name: Gaussian-type orbital
concepts.statement: A basis function made of a spherical harmonic times a Gaussian e^{−αr²}; since a product of Gaussians is a Gaussian, its matrix elements are easy to compute, and most quantum chemistry programs use them.

concepts.name: Orbital as a sum of exponentials
concepts.statement: A single-electron function written as a linear combination of exponentials with different decay constants ζ_j and adjustable coefficients c_j; the ζ_j act as effective nuclear charges, so the charge the electron feels can change with its distance from the nucleus.

concepts.name: Nonlinear variational method
concepts.statement: A variational calculation that varies a parameter inside the basis functions, such as an exponent ζ, so that the energy depends on it nonlinearly and every integral must be recomputed at each change; varying only the coefficients of fixed functions is the linear variational method, which is far cheaper.

concepts.name: Optimized Slater orbital exponents
concepts.statement: Orbital exponents optimized once by variational calculations on small systems are reused for larger ones; ζ₁s rises by about one unit per element from He to Ne, while ζ₂s,₂p rises much more slowly.

concepts.name: Perturbation theory
concepts.statement: Finding approximate energies and wavefunctions of a problem that cannot be solved exactly by writing its Hamiltonian as one whose eigenstates are known plus a small perturbation, and correcting the known solutions by a series of successive terms.

concepts.name: Perturbation series in λ
concepts.statement: The perturbed state and energy are expanded as power series in a bookkeeping parameter λ that goes with Ĥ¹ and is set to 1 at the end; the term in λ^i is of order (Ĥ¹/Ĥ⁰)^i, and truncating the series is the approximation.

concepts.name: Matching powers of λ
concepts.statement: Putting the series into (Ĥ⁰ + λĤ¹)|n⟩ = E_n|n⟩ and equating the terms of each power of λ gives back the unperturbed equation at zeroth order and, at first order, an equation that links the first-order corrections to the energy and to the state.

concepts.name: First-order energy correction
concepts.statement: The first-order change in the energy of a state is the expectation value of the perturbation in the unperturbed state, so E_n ≈ E_n⁰ + ⟨n⁰|Ĥ¹|n⁰⟩.

concepts.name: First-order wavefunction correction
concepts.statement: The first-order correction to a state is a linear combination of the other unperturbed states, each weighted by ⟨m⁰|Ĥ¹|n⁰⟩/(E_n⁰ − E_m⁰): states of comparable energy that the perturbation couples contribute most, and symmetry makes many of the weights zero.

concepts.name: When perturbation theory fails
concepts.statement: Some problems cannot be treated by perturbation theory however weak the perturbation: an arbitrarily weak attractive potential binds a free particle with a binding energy of order λ², while a repulsive one binds none, so the energy shift is not a power series in λ.

concepts.name: Atomic units
concepts.statement: The Hartree system of natural units for atomic calculations, in which the electron's mass m_e, the elementary charge e, the reduced Planck constant ħ and the Coulomb force constant 1/4πε₀ are each 1, so a quantity is written as a multiple of the atomic unit of its dimension.

concepts.name: Hartree
concepts.statement: The atomic unit of energy, E_h = m_e e⁴/(4πε₀ħ)² = 4.359 × 10⁻¹⁸ J, or 27.2 eV; it is twice the Rydberg energy.

concepts.name: Fine-structure constant
concepts.statement: The dimensionless constant α ≈ 1/137 that ties the atomic units to the speed of light: c is 1/α ≈ 137 in atomic units, a₀ = ħ/(m_e cα) and E_h = α²m_e c².

concepts.name: Helium Hamiltonian in atomic units
concepts.statement: In atomic units every constant drops out of the helium Hamiltonian, leaving Ĥ = −½(∇₁² + ∇₂²) − 2/r₁ − 2/r₂ + 1/r₁₂: the kinetic energies, the two attractions to the nucleus and the repulsion between the electrons.

concepts.name: Zero-order Hamiltonian
concepts.statement: The part Ĥ⁰ of a Hamiltonian that can be solved exactly; the rest, Ĥ¹, is treated as a correction, so Ĥ = Ĥ⁰ + Ĥ¹.

concepts.name: Perturbation treatment of helium
concepts.statement: For helium the zero-order Hamiltonian is two hydrogen-like Hamiltonians with Z = 2, solved by a product of two 1s orbitals, and the perturbation is the electron–electron repulsion Ĥ¹ = 1/r₁₂.

concepts.name: First-order energy of helium
concepts.statement: The first-order correction is the average repulsion of two electrons in the unperturbed 1s orbitals, E¹ = +34.0 eV, which raises the zero-order −108.8 eV to −74.8 eV; adding E² gives −79.2 eV, within 0.3% of experiment, and agreement within the experimental uncertainty takes thirteenth order.

concepts.name: Judging an approximation against experiment
concepts.statement: Comparing a calculated energy with the measured one through the relative deviation |(E_trial − E_exp)/E_exp|; an approximation is only as good as its agreement with experiment.

concepts.name: Electron correlation
concepts.statement: Electrons repel and tend to avoid one another, so the motion of each depends on where the others are; an orbital (product) wavefunction is uncorrelated and gives the electrons too much independence, and building their avoidance into the wavefunction lowers the energy toward experiment.

concepts.name: Variational energies of helium
concepts.statement: Five trial wavefunctions for helium give −2.84766, −2.86035, −2.87566, −2.89112 and −2.90143 E_h against the experimental −2.90372 E_h: each adds more electron–electron interaction, from one scaled 1s orbital to Chandrasekhar's three-parameter function, and the error falls from 1.93% to 0.08%.

concepts.name: Hylleraas wavefunction
concepts.statement: A trial wavefunction that puts the interelectronic distance into the function itself, ψ = e^{−α(r₁ + r₂)}(1 + βr₁₂), so the wavefunction grows when the electrons are far apart.

concepts.name: Hartree approximation
concepts.statement: The approximation of an N-electron wavefunction by a product of one-electron orbitals, each electron moving independently in the field of the nucleus and the averaged (mean-field) charge of the other N − 1 electrons.

concepts.name: Electron charge density
concepts.statement: The smooth density of the electrons summed over the occupied orbitals, ρ(r) = Σ|ψ_i(r)|², which stands in for the other electrons in the Hartree approximation.

concepts.name: Mean-field potential
concepts.statement: The potential an electron feels from the other electrons smeared out into their charge density, V_electron(r) = −e∫ρ(r′)/|r − r′| dr′, added to the nucleus's attraction.

concepts.name: Hartree equations
