concepts.statement: A form of energy made of oscillating electric and magnetic fields, perpendicular to each other and to the direction of propagation, travelling in a straight line at constant velocity, c = 2.99792 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum; refraction is best described by treating it as a wave, absorption and emission by treating it as particles.

concepts.name: Oscillating field of a light wave
concepts.statement: At any point along the propagating wave the electric field oscillates as A_t = A_e sin(2πνt + φ), with A_e its maximum amplitude, ν the number of oscillations per unit time and φ a phase angle; the magnetic field follows the identical equation with its own amplitude A_m.

concepts.name: Plane-polarized radiation
concepts.statement: Radiation with a single oscillating electric field and a single oscillating magnetic field, each in one plane; normally radiation is unpolarized, its fields present in all planes perpendicular to the direction of propagation.

concepts.name: Wavelength and frequency of light
concepts.statement: The wavelength, the distance between successive maxima, and the frequency of electromagnetic radiation are related through the speed of light, λ = c/ν; the wavenumber is the reciprocal of the wavelength, usually in cm⁻¹.

concepts.name: Electromagnetic spectrum
concepts.statement: Electromagnetic radiation divided into regions by the type of atomic or molecular transition that absorbs or emits it, from γ-rays (nuclear) through X-rays, ultraviolet and visible (electrons), infrared (molecular vibrations) and microwaves (rotations) to radio waves (spins); the boundaries are not rigid.

concepts.name: Spectroscopy by exchange of energy
concepts.statement: A spectroscopic measurement is possible only when the photon's interaction with the sample changes one of its properties; in one broad class of techniques energy passes between photon and sample by absorption, emission, photoluminescence or chemiluminescence, each region of the spectrum giving its own technique (Table 13.1.1).

concepts.name: Energy of a spectroscopic transition
concepts.statement: A transition between an upper and a lower energy level absorbs or emits radiation whose frequency matches the energy difference, ΔE = E_u − E_l = hν.

concepts.name: Spectral regions and molecular motions
concepts.statement: Microwave radiation (10⁹–10¹¹ Hz) drives transitions between rotational levels, infrared (10¹³–10¹⁴ Hz) between vibrational levels with rotational ones alongside, and visible and ultraviolet light (10¹⁴–10¹⁶ Hz) between electronic levels with vibrational and rotational ones alongside.

concepts.name: Rovibrational spectrum
concepts.statement: The spectrum of vibrational transitions coupled with rotational transitions: closely spaced rotational levels (1–10 cm⁻¹ apart) ride on vibrational levels about 1000 cm⁻¹ apart, so each vibrational band breaks into lines from which the average bond length can be found.

concepts.name: Rotational term
concepts.statement: The rotational energy divided by h or hc, F(J) = E_r/h = BJ(J + 1) in frequency or F̃(J) = E_r/hc = B̃J(J + 1) in wavenumbers; the rotational constant is written B in either unit.

concepts.name: Rovibrational term
concepts.statement: In the rigid rotor–harmonic oscillator picture the total nuclear energy is the vibrational term plus the rotational term, S(v, J) = G(v) + F(J) = ν₀(v + ½) + BJ(J + 1).

concepts.name: Rovibrational selection rules
concepts.statement: A vibrational transition changes v by ±1, and since at room temperature only v = 0 is populated, Δv = +1; the rotational quantum number must change at the same time, ΔJ = ±1, since a photon carries one quantum of angular momentum, so the pure vibrational line (ΔJ = 0) is not observed in most cases.

concepts.name: R branch
concepts.statement: The lines with ΔJ = +1, labelled R(J) by the lower level's J, at ΔE = hν₀ + 2hB(J + 1), J = 0, 1, 2, …, on the high-energy side of the band.

concepts.name: P branch
concepts.statement: The lines with ΔJ = −1, labelled P(J) by the lower level's J, at ΔE = hν₀ − 2hBJ, J = 1, 2, 3, …, on the low-energy side of the band.

concepts.name: Q branch
concepts.statement: Lines with ΔJ = 0 would all fall at the band origin, ΔE = hν₀; the Q branch is observed in polyatomic molecules and in diatomics with electronic angular momentum in the ground state, such as NO, and is absent in most diatomics.

concepts.name: Zero gap
concepts.statement: In the rigid rotor–harmonic oscillator picture the P and R lines are equally spaced, 2B apart, while P(1) and R(0) are 4B apart, the gap where the Q branch would stand; the spacing gives the bond length without pure rotational spectroscopy.

concepts.name: Boltzmann distribution
concepts.statement: In thermal equilibrium at temperature T the number of molecules in a level relative to another falls off as the Boltzmann factor e^(−ΔE/kT) of their energy difference, multiplied by the level's degeneracy.

concepts.name: Rotational populations
concepts.statement: The population of rotational level J relative to J = 0 is N_J/N₀ = (2J + 1)e^(−E_r/kT): the degeneracy grows with J and the exponential falls, so the population peaks at J_max = (kT/2hB)^½ − ½ and shifts to higher J in heavier molecules and at higher temperature.

concepts.name: Intensities of rovibrational lines
concepts.statement: The relative intensity of each P or R line is set by the population of its lower J level, so the lines rise to a maximum and fall away as J grows; the overall intensity of the band depends on the vibrational transition dipole moment.

concepts.name: Vibration–rotation interaction
concepts.statement: The bond length grows with the vibrational state because higher states have larger amplitudes and the anharmonic well lets the bond stretch further; since B̃ = h/8π²cμR_e² falls as the bond lengthens, the rotational constant depends on v, B̃_v, with B̃₁ < B̃₀.

concepts.name: Branch lines with a vibration-dependent B
concepts.statement: With B̃_v in the term values, the v = 0 → 1 lines lie at ν̃_R = ν̃ + 2B̃₁ + (3B̃₁ − B̃₀)J + (B̃₁ − B̃₀)J² for J = 0, 1, 2, … and ν̃_P = ν̃ − (B̃₁ + B̃₀)J + (B̃₁ − B̃₀)J² for J = 1, 2, 3, ….

concepts.name: Unequal spacing of the branches
concepts.statement: Because B̃₁ − B̃₀ is negative, the J² term pulls the R lines closer together as J increases and pushes the P lines further apart, so real rovibrational spectra lose the equal 2B̃ spacing.

concepts.name: Centrifugal force
concepts.statement: The force that, in a rotating molecule, tends to fly the reduced mass away from the axis of rotation, F_c = μr_cω² = L²/μr_c³.

concepts.name: Non-rigid rotor
concepts.statement: A rotating molecule whose bond is elastic: the bond stretches from r_e to r_c until the restoring force k(r_c − r_e) balances the centrifugal force, and the work done is stored as potential energy, so the rotational energy is kinetic plus potential.

concepts.name: Levels of the non-rigid rotor
concepts.statement: The rotational terms of a non-rigid rotor are F(J) = B̃J(J + 1) − D̃J²(J + 1)², the rigid-rotor term less a centrifugal stretching term, so each level lies slightly lower than the rigid rotor's, more so as J grows.

concepts.name: Centrifugal distortion constant
concepts.statement: The constant D̃ = ħ³/4πkμ²r_e⁶c (in cm⁻¹) of the centrifugal stretching term; it measures the influence of the centrifugal force and, through the force constant k, the interaction of rotation and vibration, and is very small beside B̃ (for HCl about 0.0004 against 10.4 cm⁻¹).

concepts.name: Line spacing of a non-rigid rotor
concepts.statement: With ΔJ = ±1 the rotational lines of a non-rigid rotor draw closer together as J increases, unlike the even spacing of the rigid rotor; the effect is significant only at large J since D̃ ≪ B̃.

concepts.name: Hot band
concepts.statement: A transition starting from an excited vibrational level, such as 1 → n, which appears when the sample is warm enough to populate v = 1.

concepts.name: Selection rule of the anharmonic oscillator
concepts.statement: For the anharmonic oscillator Δv may be any number, so overtones 0 → 2, 0 → 3, … appear beside the fundamental, their probability falling rapidly as Δv grows.

concepts.name: Positions of the overtones
concepts.statement: Because the anharmonic levels close up as v increases, an overtone lies below the whole multiple of the fundamental that the harmonic oscillator predicts, increasingly so for higher overtones (HCl: 5668.0 against 5771.8 cm⁻¹ for 0 → 2).

concepts.name: Vibronic transition
concepts.statement: An electronic transition accompanied by vibrational (and rotational) transitions, drawn as a jump between two electronic potential curves with their vibrational levels; the rotational part is usually small enough to ignore.

concepts.name: Electronic term
concepts.statement: The electronic energy change of a transition in wavenumbers, ν̃_el or T̃_el, measured between the minima of the two electronic potential curves.

concepts.name: Total energy of a diatomic molecule
concepts.statement: In the anharmonic oscillator–non-rigid rotor picture the energy of a diatomic, translation excluded, is the electronic term plus the vibrational and rotational terms, Ẽ_total = ν̃_el + G(v) + F(J), with ν̃_e and χ̃_e depending on the electronic state.

concepts.name: Wavenumber of a vibronic band
concepts.statement: From the v″ = 0 level of the lower state, rotation ignored, a band lands at ν̃_obs = T̃_el + (½ν̃′_e − ¼χ̃′_eν̃′_e) − (½ν̃″_e − ¼χ̃″_eν̃″_e) + ν̃′_ev′ − χ̃′_eν̃′_ev′(v′ + 1), which depends mainly on the upper state's constants.

concepts.name: 0–0 transition
concepts.statement: The transition between the v = 0 levels of the two states, ν̃₀₀ = T̃_el + (½ν̃′_e − ¼χ̃′_eν̃′_e) − (½ν̃″_e − ¼χ̃″_eν̃″_e), the lowest energy observable in an electronic band, though possibly weak.

concepts.name: Bands, lines and band heads
concepts.statement: In an electronic spectrum each peak from one vibrational level to another is a band, made of hundreds of rotational lines; the region of maximum absorption where many lines fall together is the band head, and the set of all bands of one electronic transition is a band system.

concepts.name: Convergence limit
concepts.statement: As v′ increases the spacing of the upper state's levels, and so of the bands, falls to zero at the convergence limit, beyond which the spectrum is continuous because the excited molecule is not bound; the energy to dissociate it is D₀′, not D_e′, because it cannot have less than the zero-point energy.

concepts.name: Franck–Condon principle
concepts.statement: An electronic transition is so fast compared with nuclear motion that the nuclear configuration does not change during it; the nuclei then find themselves out of equilibrium in the new electronic state and must vibrate. In its quantum form, the intensity of a vibronic transition is proportional to the square of the overlap of the vibrational wavefunctions of the two states.

concepts.name: Condon approximation
concepts.statement: The assumption that the electronic transition occurs on a time scale short compared to nuclear motion, so that the transition probability can be calculated at a fixed nuclear position.

concepts.name: Vertical transition
concepts.statement: A transition drawn as a vertical line from the lower potential curve to the upper one at an unchanged internuclear distance, as the Franck–Condon principle requires.

concepts.name: Franck–Condon factor
concepts.statement: Since the transition dipole acts only on the electrons, the Born–Oppenheimer transition moment factors into the nuclear overlap ⟨ψ_nuc,f|ψ_nuc,i⟩ times the electronic moment; the probability of a vibronic transition is weighted by the square of that overlap, and a transition whose overlap is zero is not observed.

concepts.name: Gaussian integral
concepts.statement: The integral of a Gaussian over the whole line, ∫ e^(−z²) dz = √π from −∞ to ∞, found from a table of integrals.

concepts.name: Overlaps of displaced oscillators
concepts.statement: For harmonic wells of the same α = √(mk)/ħ with minima at R_e and Q_e, the v = 0 functions overlap by S₀₀ = e^(−α(R_e−Q_e)²/4), and v = 0 with the upper v′ = 1 by S₀₁ = √(α/2)(R_e − Q_e)e^(−α(R_e−Q_e)²/4).

concepts.name: Franck–Condon progression
concepts.statement: An absorption band made of transitions from v = 0 to the successive upper levels, each with its own overlap and energy; a small displacement of the upper well leaves the 0–0 band strongest, a large one moves the maximum to higher levels, and so the band's shape tells whether the equilibrium bond length changed.

concepts.name: Homogeneous and inhomogeneous broadening
concepts.statement: Spectral lines are not infinitely narrow: the finite lifetime of a state broadens every molecule's line alike (homogeneous broadening), and small differences in each molecule's environment spread them further (inhomogeneous broadening).

concepts.name: Bond length in the excited state
concepts.statement: When an electron moves from a bonding orbital to a non-bonding or antibonding one, the bond order is lower in the excited state and the equilibrium bond length grows, Q_e > R_e.

concepts.name: Inertia tensor
concepts.statement: The 3 × 3 matrix of moments of inertia of a body in lab-based Cartesian coordinates, I_xx = Σm_k(y_k² + z_k²), …, with products of inertia I_xy = −Σm_kx_ky_k, …; it is real and symmetric.

concepts.name: Principal moments of inertia
concepts.statement: The diagonal moments I_a, I_b, I_c of the inertia tensor in molecule-fixed axes a, b, c, labelled so that I_a < I_b < I_c.

concepts.name: Rotational Hamiltonian of a polyatomic molecule
concepts.statement: The rotational kinetic energy operator of a rigid non-linear molecule, H_rot = J_a²/2I_a + J_b²/2I_b + J_c²/2I_c, in terms of the angular momentum components along the principal axes.

concepts.name: Euler angles
concepts.statement: The three angles θ, φ and χ that specify the orientation of a rigid molecule relative to a laboratory-fixed coordinate system.

concepts.name: Spherical top
concepts.statement: A molecule whose three principal moments of inertia are equal, so that H_rot = J²/2I and its eigenfunctions are those of J², J_a and J_Z.

concepts.name: Levels of a spherical top
concepts.statement: A spherical top has E = ħ²J(J + 1)/2I, independent of K and M, each ranging from −J to J, so each level is (2J + 1)²-fold degenerate.

concepts.name: Symmetric top
concepts.statement: A molecule with two equal principal moments of inertia and one different: an oblate top (a frisbee) when the unique axis has the greater moment, a prolate top (a football) when it has the smaller.

concepts.name: Levels of a symmetric top
concepts.statement: With J² and the component along the unique axis, a prolate top has E = ħ²J(J + 1)/2I + ħ²K²(1/2I_a − 1/2I) and an oblate top the same with I_c; the energy depends on K, so each level is only (2J + 1)-fold degenerate.

concepts.name: Symmetric-top wavefunctions
concepts.statement: The eigenfunctions |J, M, K⟩ = √((2J + 1)/8π²) D*_{J,M,K}(θ, φ, χ) of J², J_Z and J_a, with eigenvalues ħ²J(J + 1), ħM and ħK, given by the rotation matrices.

concepts.name: Asymmetric top
concepts.statement: A molecule whose three principal moments differ has no closed-form levels: H_rot is set up as a matrix in the |J, M, K⟩ basis and diagonalized; J still commutes with H_rot, so each eigenstate keeps one J.

concepts.name: Kinds of vibrational motion
concepts.statement: The internal motions of a group of atoms are named by their pattern: symmetric and asymmetric stretching, which change bond lengths, and wagging, twisting, scissoring and rocking, which change angles in or out of the plane.

concepts.name: Harmonic potential of a polyatomic molecule
concepts.statement: Near equilibrium, anharmonic terms neglected, the potential energy of a molecule's vibrations is the quadratic form ΔV = ½ΣΣ f_ij q_iq_j of the displacements, with force constants f_ij = ∂²V/∂q_i∂q_j.

concepts.name: Normal coordinates
concepts.statement: A set of coordinates Q_j, found by matrix algebra, in which the potential has no cross terms, ΔV = ½ΣF_jQ_j²; each follows the path of one normal mode, an independent motion of the atoms orthogonal to the others.

concepts.name: Separation of the vibrations
concepts.statement: In normal coordinates the vibrational Hamiltonian is a sum of independent harmonic oscillators, Ĥ_vib = ΣĤ_vib,j, so the vibrational wavefunction is a product of one-mode wavefunctions and each mode can be treated as a harmonic oscillator.

concepts.name: Vibrational energy of a polyatomic molecule
concepts.statement: The total vibrational energy is the sum of the energies of the N_vib independent oscillators, E_vib = Σhν_j(v_j + ½), v_j = 0, 1, 2, ….

concepts.name: Symmetry of a normal mode
concepts.statement: Every normal coordinate, and the vibrational wavefunctions that go with it, forms a basis for an irreducible representation of the molecule's point group, which decides whether the mode is IR or Raman active.

concepts.name: Assigning a mode's symmetry species
concepts.statement: Apply each symmetry operation of the point group to a mode's displacement arrows, write +1 where they go to themselves and −1 where they reverse, and match the row to the character table: water's three modes give Γ_vib = 2a₁ + b₂.

concepts.name: Time-dependent perturbation theory
concepts.statement: Dirac's method for the effect of a time-dependent perturbation V(t) on a system with a time-independent Hamiltonian H₀, H = H₀ + H₁(t): since the energy levels and eigenstates of the perturbed system change in time, it asks for time-dependent expectation values and for the time-dependent amplitudes of the unperturbed eigenstates.

concepts.name: Amplitudes
concepts.statement: The complex coefficients c_n(t) of the unperturbed eigenstates in |ψ(t)⟩ = Σc_n(t)e^(−iE_nt/ħ)|n⟩, with the phase factors taken out so that without a perturbation they stay constant; |c_n(t)|² is the probability that the system is in state n at time t.

concepts.name: Equations for the amplitudes
concepts.statement: Substituting the expansion into the time-dependent Schrödinger equation gives ∂c_n/∂t = (−i/ħ)Σ_k⟨n|H₁(t)|k⟩c_k(t)e^(−i(E_k−E_n)t/ħ): the matrix elements of H₁ shift amplitude between states, and the phase factor modulates the direction of the shift.

concepts.name: Two-level system
concepts.statement: A system of two states |1⟩ and |2⟩ coupled by a perturbation, whose amplitudes obey iħ ∂c₁/∂t = c₁H₁₁ + c₂e^(−iω₀t)H₁₂ and iħ ∂c₂/∂t = c₂H₂₂ + c₁e^(iω₀t)H₂₁.

forms.latex: i \hbar \dfrac{\partial c_1(t)}{\partial t} = c_1(t) H_{11}(t) + c_2 e^{-i \omega_0 t} H_{12} (t)
i \hbar \dfrac{\partial c_2(t)}{\partial t} = c_2(t) H_{22}(t) + c_1 e^{+i \omega_0 t} H_{21} (t)

concepts.name: First-order amplitude of the upper state
concepts.statement: Starting in |1⟩ with H₁₁ = H₂₂ = 0, to first order c₂(t) = (−i/ħ)∫₀ᵗ e^(iω₀t′)H₂₁(t′)dt′; for light H₁(t) = V cos ωt near resonance, ω ≈ ω₀, this is c₂(t) = −(i/ħ)H₂₁e^(i(ω₀−ω)t/2) sin[(ω − ω₀)t/2]/(ω − ω₀).

concepts.name: Transition probability
concepts.statement: The probability of finding the system in |2⟩ after time t, P₁₂(t) = |c₂(t)|² = |H₂₁|² sin²[(ω − ω₀)t/2]/ħ²(ω − ω₀)², oscillates in time; as a function of ω it peaks at ω = ω₀ with height |H₁₂t/2ħ|² and width 4π/t, growing higher and narrower until first-order theory breaks down, since P₁₂ cannot exceed 1.

concepts.name: Resonance condition
concepts.statement: Light causes appreciable transitions between two stationary states only when its frequency is nearly equal to their energy difference, ω ≈ ω₀ = (E₂ − E₁)/ħ, and the transition is fullest when the perturbation is turned off after π/|ω − ω₀| or an odd multiple of it.

concepts.name: Gross and specific selection rules
concepts.statement: A selection rule has two parts: the gross selection rule, a requirement the atom or molecule must meet to show a spectrum of a given kind (a permanent dipole for a microwave spectrum), and the specific selection rule, which says which changes of quantum number may happen.

concepts.name: Light couples through the transition dipole
concepts.statement: Incident radiation presents an oscillating electric field E₀ cos ωt that interacts with the transition dipole (μ_z)₁₂ = ∫Ψ₁*μ_zΨ₂dτ, a transient polarization created by the radiation; if it is zero the transition is forbidden.

concepts.name: Recurrence of the associated Legendre functions
concepts.statement: x times an associated Legendre function is a combination of its two neighbours in J: (2J + 1)xP_J^{|M|}(x) = (J − |M| + 1)P_{J+1}^{|M|}(x) + (J + |M|)P_{J−1}^{|M|}(x).

concepts.name: Transition moment of the rigid rotor
concepts.statement: For z-polarized light the rotor's transition moment, an integral of two spherical harmonics with μ cos θ, vanishes unless the molecule has a permanent dipole, M′ = M and J′ = J ± 1; the same rules apply to orbital angular momentum (Δl = ±1, Δm = 0).

concepts.name: A vibration must change the dipole
concepts.statement: If the dipole moment did not change during a vibration it could be taken out of M(v → v′) = ⟨φ(v′)|μ|φ(0)⟩, leaving the overlap of two orthogonal vibrational functions, zero; so a transition is IR allowed only if the dipole moment changes, which is why homonuclear diatomics have no IR spectrum, and Raman allowed only if the polarizability changes.

concepts.name: Separating stretches from bends
concepts.statement: Draw a double-headed arrow on each bond, find how the arrows transform under each operation to get Γ_stretch, reduce it, and take Γ_bend = Γ_vib − Γ_stretch: water has Γ_stretch = a₁ + b₂ and Γ_bend = a₁.

concepts.name: Spin of the proton and neutron
concepts.statement: The proton and neutron, like the electron, have spin ½ and belong to the fermions, the particles governed by the Pauli exclusion principle.

concepts.name: Spin and orbital angular momentum compared
concepts.statement: An intrinsic spin angular momentum is possessed in addition to the orbital one, the two analogous to the daily and annual motions of the Earth around the Sun; the spin quantum numbers s and m_s take the place of ℓ and m, and a complete theory of spin requires relativistic quantum mechanics.

concepts.name: Local magnetic field
concepts.statement: The magnetic field felt by a particular nucleus in a molecule: the applied field B induces currents in the surrounding electrons, so the field at the nucleus is slightly lower or slightly higher than the external field, B_loc = B + δB = (1 − σ)B.

concepts.name: Shielded nucleus
concepts.statement: A nucleus is shielded when the magnetic field it experiences is lower than the external magnetic field, B_y < B_x.

concepts.name: Deshielded nucleus
concepts.statement: A nucleus is deshielded when the magnetic field it experiences is higher than the external magnetic field, B_y > B_x.

concepts.name: Shielding constant
concepts.statement: The constant σ by which shielding reduces the local magnetic field, B_loc = (1 − σ)B.

concepts.name: Larmor frequency
concepts.statement: A nucleus of magnetogyric ratio γ resonates at its Larmor frequency, ν_L = γB_loc/2π for a shielded nucleus, the frequency with which its magnetic moment precesses about the field; in angular units ω = −γB₀.

concepts.name: Chemical shift
concepts.statement: The difference between the resonance frequency of a nucleus and that of a standard, reported on the δ-scale in parts per million, δ = (ν − ν₀)/ν₀ × 10⁶; it gives vital information about the local structure surrounding the nucleus.

concepts.name: Contributions to the shielding constant
concepts.statement: The shielding constant is the sum of three contributions, σ = σ(local) + σ(molecule) + σ(solvent): from the electrons on the atom that contains the nucleus, from the rest of the molecule, and from surrounding solvent molecules.

concepts.name: Diamagnetic shielding
concepts.statement: The part σ_d of the local contribution to the shielding that arises from circulation of the electrons in response to the applied field.

concepts.name: Paramagnetic shielding
concepts.statement: The part σ_p of the local contribution to the shielding, which with the diamagnetic part σ_d makes up the local contribution.

concepts.name: Lamb formula
concepts.statement: The magnitude of the diamagnetic shielding is σ_d = (e²μ₀/3m_e)∫₀^∞ ρ(r) r dr, with ρ the electron probability density; σ_d is inversely proportional to the Bohr radius.

concepts.name: Magnetic susceptibility
concepts.statement: The property χ of a group to which the currents an applied magnetic field generates in it are proportional.

concepts.name: Molecular contribution to the shielding
concepts.statement: The applied field generates currents in neighbouring groups in proportion to their magnetic susceptibility; the induced magnetic moment gives rise to a field at the nucleus inversely proportional to the cube of its distance.

concepts.name: Spin-spin coupling
concepts.statement: The magnetic interaction between neighbouring, non-equivalent NMR-active nuclei: each proton feels the small field of its neighbour, aligned with B₀ in about half the molecules and against it in the rest, so its signal is split into subpeaks, one upfield and one downfield of the original signal.

concepts.name: Singlets, doublets, triplets and quartets
concepts.statement: An unsplit signal is a singlet; one split into two subpeaks of equal height is a doublet; into three, with the middle peak twice the area of each outer one, a triplet; into four, with the two middle peaks taller, a quartet.

concepts.name: Drawing a splitting diagram
concepts.statement: Draw the unsplit signal as a line and split it once for each coupled neighbour, half the subpeaks shifted upfield and half downfield; with two different couplings it is usually easier to show the larger splitting first, then the finer one.

concepts.name: Intensities of the subpeaks
concepts.statement: The subpeak areas follow the number of equally probable arrangements of the neighbours' spins: 1:1 for a doublet, 1:2:1 for a triplet, since the two mixed arrangements cancel, and 1:3:3:1 for a quartet, the rows of Pascal's triangle.

concepts.name: The n + 1 rule
concepts.statement: A set of hydrogens with n neighbouring, non-equivalent hydrogens is split into n + 1 subpeaks; the rule is empirical and applies to first-order spectra.

concepts.name: Equivalent hydrogens do not split each other
concepts.statement: Signal splitting only occurs between non-equivalent hydrogens: equivalent hydrogens do not split one another's signals, an observed fact.

concepts.name: Coupling through three bonds
concepts.statement: Splitting occurs primarily between hydrogens separated by three bonds; four- and five-bond coupling is occasionally seen and much weaker, and hydrogens on heteroatoms couple weakly or not at all because they exchange rapidly with solvent or other molecules.

concepts.name: Coupling constant
concepts.statement: The difference J, expressed in Hz, between two adjacent subpeaks in a split signal, written ³J_a-b for a three-bond coupling between H_a and H_b.

concepts.name: Coupling constants do not depend on the field
concepts.statement: Unlike the chemical shift, the coupling constant expressed in Hz is the same regardless of the applied field strength, because the magnetic moment of the neighbouring proton does not depend on the applied field.

concepts.name: Reciprocal coupling constants
concepts.statement: The coupling between two sets of hydrogens has the same magnitude in either direction: H_a splits H_b by the same J that H_b splits H_a, which helps identify coupling partners.

concepts.name: Typical coupling constants
concepts.statement: Protons on neighbouring sp³ carbons couple at about 6–8 Hz; vinylic trans hydrogens at 11–18 Hz, cis at 6–15 Hz and geminal at 5 Hz or lower; ortho hydrogens on a benzene ring at 6–10 Hz, meta up to 4 Hz; an aldehyde proton and a three-bond neighbour at 2–3 Hz.

concepts.name: Complex coupling
concepts.statement: The splitting of a set of hydrogens coupled to two or more sets of non-equivalent neighbours with different coupling constants.

concepts.name: Doublet of doublets
concepts.statement: The four-line pattern of a proton split into a doublet by one neighbour and each subpeak split again into a doublet by another with a different coupling constant; abbreviated dd.

concepts.name: Overlapping subpeaks
concepts.statement: When a proton is coupled to two non-equivalent sets with identical or very close coupling constants, its subpeaks overlap and the pattern appears to follow the n + 1 rule: a triplet of doublets looks like a quartet, a triplet of quartets like a sextet.

concepts.name: Multiplet
concepts.statement: A signal, or a group of overlapping signals of very similar chemical shift, whose splitting pattern is too complex to analyse in detail.

concepts.name: Stronger magnets resolve more
concepts.statement: The stronger the magnet, the more resolution in the spectrum: the 12 ppm window of proton signals is 1200 Hz wide at 100 MHz (about 2.4 T) and 6000 Hz at 500 MHz (about 12 T), while coupling constants stay the same in Hz.

concepts.name: Nuclear spin operators
concepts.statement: Î_i is the operator for the spin angular momentum of nucleus i and Î_iz for its projection along the z-axis; for a spin-½ nucleus Î_iz|α_i⟩ = ½|α_i⟩ and Î_iz|β_i⟩ = −½|β_i⟩, with ħ set to 1.

concepts.name: Hamiltonian of two coupled spins
concepts.statement: The Hamiltonian of two coupled nuclear spins is Ĥ = ω₁Î₁z + ω₂Î₂z + (2πJ₁₂/ħ)(Î₁·Î₂), the Larmor terms of each nucleus plus the coupling; in frequency units with ħ = 1 it is Ĥ = ν₁Î₁z + ν₂Î₂z + J₁₂(Î₁·Î₂).

concepts.name: Shift operators
concepts.statement: The operators Î_i± = Î_ix ± iÎ_iy, which raise or lower a spin: Î_i+|β_i⟩ = |α_i⟩, Î_i+|α_i⟩ = 0, Î_i−|α_i⟩ = |β_i⟩, Î_i−|β_i⟩ = 0.

concepts.name: Scalar product of two spins
concepts.statement: The scalar product of two spin operators, written with the shift operators: Î₁·Î₂ = (Î₁₊Î₂₋ + Î₁₋Î₂₊)/2 + Î₁zÎ₂z.

concepts.name: Hamiltonian matrix of two equivalent spins
concepts.statement: In the basis of product functions |α₁α₂⟩, |α₁β₂⟩, |β₁α₂⟩, |β₁β₂⟩ the Hamiltonian of two equivalent spins is a matrix with diagonal ν + J/4, −J/4, −J/4, −ν + J/4 and J/2 coupling the two mixed states.

concepts.name: Triplet and singlet states of two spins
concepts.statement: The eigenstates of two equivalent coupled spins are the triplet |α₁α₂⟩, (|α₁β₂⟩ + |β₁α₂⟩)/√2, |β₁β₂⟩ with energies ν + J/4, J/4, −ν + J/4, and the singlet (|α₁β₂⟩ − |β₁α₂⟩)/√2 with energy −3J/4.

concepts.name: Clebsch–Gordan series
concepts.statement: Two angular momenta I₁ and I₂ couple to an overall angular momentum I = I₁ + I₂ whose allowed values are I = I₁ + I₂, I₁ + I₂ − 1, …, |I₁ − I₂|, each with projections M_I = I, I − 1, …, −I; two spin-½ nuclei give a triplet (I = 1) and a singlet (I = 0).

concepts.name: Hamiltonian of the NMR transition
concepts.statement: The Hamiltonian for the process that induces an NMR transition, a magnetic field along the x-axis: Ĥ′ = ω′(Î₁ₓ + Î₂ₓ) = ω′Îₓ, with ω′ set by the strength B₁ of that field.

concepts.name: NMR selection rules
concepts.statement: The intensity of a transition is proportional to the square of ⟨ψ_f|Ĥ′|ψ_i⟩; for two coupled spins it is non-zero only for ΔI = 0 and ΔM_I = ±1, so transitions to and from the singlet state are forbidden.

concepts.name: Why equivalent protons show one line
concepts.statement: For two equivalent coupled spins the allowed transitions |4⟩ ↔ |2⟩ and |2⟩ ↔ |1⟩ both have energy ν, so only one line is observed: the coupling moves the levels but not the transition energies.

concepts.name: Magnetic and chemical equivalence
concepts.statement: Magnetically equivalent nuclei do couple to each other, but no splitting is observed; chemically equivalent but magnetically non-equivalent nuclei couple, and their coupling is observable in the spectrum.

concepts.name: AX spin system
concepts.statement: Two distinct nuclei with a spin-spin interaction between them in addition to their chemical shifts: the J coupling moves the levels up and down so that each nucleus's two transitions differ, δ + J/2 and δ − J/2, and each signal is a doublet.

concepts.name: A₂ spin system
concepts.statement: Two magnetically identical nuclei: the interaction between their spins is still present, but their spin states must be combined into states symmetric or antisymmetric to exchange, and the selection rules make the splitting unobservable.

concepts.name: Liouville–von Neumann equation
concepts.statement: The fundamental equation describing NMR quantum mechanically, neglecting relaxation: in frequency units the density matrix evolves as dρ̂/dt = −i[Ĥ, ρ̂].

concepts.name: Coupling does not affect the signal of equivalent spins
concepts.statement: For two spins with identical chemical shifts, the coupling J(Î₁·Î₂) commutes with Î₁χ + Î₂χ (χ = x, y, z), the density matrix after a 90 degree pulse, so the coupling does not influence the signal.

concepts.name: Multiplicity of a peak
concepts.statement: The number of lines a peak is split into: one for a singlet, two for a doublet, three for a triplet; for a nucleus coupled to n equivalent nuclei it is n + 1, and Pascal's triangle gives the splitting pattern.

concepts.name: Coupling to several sets of nuclei
concepts.statement: For a nucleus coupled to more than one set of equivalent nuclei, the n + 1 rule is applied independently to each set and the multiplicities multiply: coupled to two single, non-equivalent neighbours, a peak has 2 × 2 = 4 lines, a doublet of a doublet.

concepts.name: Predicting a splitting pattern
concepts.statement: Sort the hydrogens into sets of equivalent nuclei, count each set's vicinal non-equivalent neighbours, apply the n + 1 rule to each coupling set, and order the splittings by the size of their coupling constants (for alkenyl hydrogens, J_trans > J_cis > J_gem).

concepts.name: Diamagnetism
concepts.statement: A molecule whose electron spins are all paired is diamagnetic: its spins give it no magnetic moment, unlike a free radical, whose unpaired electrons do. Most molecules are diamagnetic in their ground state.

concepts.name: Singlet and triplet excited states
concepts.statement: When one electron is promoted to a higher level, it keeps its spin paired with the electron left behind in an excited singlet state (S = 0, multiplicity 2S + 1 = 1) or turns parallel to it in a triplet excited state (S = 1, multiplicity 3). The singlet ground state is diamagnetic and the triplet paramagnetic.

concepts.name: Spin-forbidden transitions
concepts.statement: A transition between a singlet and a triplet state breaks the spin selection rule ΔS = 0, so it is unlikely: singlet–triplet absorption bands are weak, and the triplet state lives about 10⁴ times longer than the singlet.

concepts.name: Fluorescence
concepts.statement: Radiative decay of an excited molecule without a change in spin multiplicity, from S₁ to S₀. It is fast, with lifetimes of 10⁻⁹ to 10⁻⁶ s.

concepts.name: Phosphorescence
concepts.statement: Radiative decay with a change in spin multiplicity, from T₁ to S₀, reached after intersystem crossing. Because the transition is spin-forbidden it is slow, taking from milliseconds to minutes or longer.

concepts.name: Jablonski diagram
concepts.statement: An energy diagram of a molecule's states, energy on the vertical axis, with one column per spin multiplicity (S₀, S₁, S₂ … and T₁, T₂ …): bold lines mark the electronic states and thin lines their vibrational levels; straight arrows are radiative transitions and wavy arrows nonradiative ones.

concepts.name: Competing deactivation processes
concepts.statement: An excited molecule returns to the ground state by several possible routes, and the favoured one is the fastest; when a radiationless path has the more favourable rate constant, fluorescence is weak or absent.

concepts.name: Vibrational relaxation
concepts.statement: The loss of vibrational energy within one electronic state, by collisions that hand vibrational quanta to other molecules or, in a large molecule, by flow into distant bonds and angles. It brings an excited molecule down to the lowest vibrational level of its electronic state in 10⁻¹² to 10⁻¹⁰ s, faster than fluorescence.

concepts.name: Red shift of fluorescence
concepts.statement: Excitation usually lands in an excited vibrational level of the excited state (the Franck–Condon principle), and vibrational relaxation outpaces emission, so fluorescence starts from the lowest level: its photon has less energy and a longer wavelength than the one absorbed.

concepts.name: Absorption and fluorescence spectra
concepts.statement: Absorption starts from the lowest vibrational level of the ground state (v″ = 0) and reaches the excited state's vibrational levels; fluorescence starts from the lowest level of the excited state (v′ = 0) and ends on the ground state's levels. The fluorescence lines therefore lie at longer wavelengths than the absorption lines.

concepts.name: Radiationless transition
concepts.statement: A transition between states that releases no photon: the energy goes into vibrations and, finally, heat.

concepts.name: Internal conversion
concepts.statement: A radiationless transition from an excited electronic state to a lower one of the same multiplicity: where the excited state's low vibrational levels overlap the high ones of the lower state, the molecule slides across and keeps dropping one vibrational level at a time. Much absorbed light ends as heat this way.

concepts.name: Intersystem crossing
concepts.statement: A radiationless crossing from a singlet excited state into a triplet state of lower energy (or back), reached by vibrational relaxation since it involves no photon. It gives access to triplet states, whose unpaired electrons react by radical processes, that light cannot reach directly.

concepts.name: External conversion
concepts.statement: Deactivation of an excited state by energy transfer to the solvent or solutes in collisions. Low temperature and high viscosity reduce the collisions and so enhance fluorescence.

concepts.name: Timescales of excitation and relaxation
concepts.statement: Absorbing a photon takes about 10⁻¹⁵ s; internal conversion 10⁻¹⁴ to 10⁻¹¹ s; vibrational relaxation 10⁻¹² to 10⁻¹⁰ s; intersystem crossing 10⁻¹¹ to 10⁻⁶ s; fluorescence 10⁻⁹ to 10⁻⁶ s; phosphorescence 10⁻³ to 100 s.

concepts.name: Population of a level
concepts.statement: The number of atoms, or their number per unit volume, in a given energy state: N₁ in the lower and N₂ in the upper level of a two-level atom.

concepts.name: Absorption
concepts.statement: A photon of energy E₂ − E₁ = hν₁₂ is absorbed and the atom goes from level 1 to level 2. Atoms leave level 1 at the rate B₁₂ρ_ν(ν₁₂)N₁.

concepts.name: Spontaneous emission
concepts.statement: An atom in level 2 decays to level 1 without outside influence, emitting a photon of energy E₂ − E₁ = hν₂₁; the photons come out over a narrow spread of frequencies, the spectral linewidth. Atoms leave level 2 at the rate A₂₁N₂.

concepts.name: Stimulated emission
concepts.statement: A photon at the transition's frequency passing an atom in level 2 induces it to emit a second photon, with the same frequency, direction and phase as the first, which continues unaffected; thermodynamically it is negative absorption. Atoms are driven down at the rate B₂₁ρ_ν(ν₂₁)N₂.

concepts.name: Laser
concepts.statement: Light amplification by the stimulated emission of radiation: a source whose light is made, and amplified, by stimulated emission.

concepts.name: Populations of two levels in thermal equilibrium
concepts.statement: At temperature T the lower level outnumbers the upper by the Boltzmann factor of their energy difference, weighted by their degeneracies. At room temperature, where k_BT is about 1/40 eV, a 1 eV gap leaves e⁴⁰ ≈ 2.4 × 10¹⁷ times more atoms in the lower level.

concepts.name: No amplification at thermal equilibrium
concepts.statement: A photon is as likely to be absorbed by an atom in the lower level as to stimulate emission from one in the upper level, but in thermal equilibrium far more atoms sit in the lower level, so light is absorbed far more often than it is amplified: no laser.

concepts.name: Einstein coefficients
concepts.statement: The proportionality constants of Einstein's rate equations: B₁₂ for absorption and B₂₁ for stimulated emission (in m³ J⁻¹ s⁻²), each multiplying the spectral radiant energy density ρ_ν and the population of the starting level, and A₂₁ (in s⁻¹), the probability per unit time of spontaneous emission.

concepts.name: Rate equation of a two-level system
concepts.statement: With light of the right frequency present, absorption, spontaneous emission and stimulated emission go on at once, and the populations change at the net rate of the three.

concepts.name: Relations between the Einstein coefficients
concepts.statement: Requiring the rate equation at thermal equilibrium to give Planck's distribution fixes A₂₁/B₂₁ = 8πhν₁₂³/c³ and g₁B₁₂ = g₂B₂₁, so one coefficient gives the other two.

concepts.name: Rate equation in the net upper population
concepts.statement: With g₁B₁₂ = g₂B₂₁ the upper level's rate equation collects into spontaneous emission plus a stimulated term proportional to the net upper population N₂ − (g₂/g₁)N₁.

concepts.name: Population inversion
concepts.statement: A state in which the net upper population N₂ − (g₂/g₁)N₁ is positive, so that light is amplified rather than absorbed; optical amplification and lasing occur only then. It needs energy supplied to the system by optical, electrical or thermal means.

concepts.name: Properties of laser light
concepts.statement: A laser's light should be coherent, its photons in phase with one another; monochromatic, of one frequency; and collimated, a sharp pencil-like beam; and the laser should be efficient.

concepts.name: Efficiency of a laser
concepts.statement: The ratio of a laser's output energy to its input energy. A typical He–Ne laser's is near 0.1 %: 1 mW of light for every watt drawn.

concepts.name: Metastable state
concepts.statement: A long-lived excited state, with lifetimes typically in the milliseconds, in which atoms can wait for a passing photon to stimulate their emission before they decay spontaneously; the upper lasing state must be one.

concepts.name: Stimulated emission must outpace absorption
concepts.statement: Lasing needs the rate of stimulated emission to exceed the rate of absorption; with B₂₁ = B₁₂ and the same spectral energy density, that is N₂ > N₁, a population inversion.

concepts.name: Pumping
concepts.statement: Supplying energy to the gain medium to raise its atoms into the excited state from which they lase: by an intense light (a flash lamp or another laser), an electric current or a discharge.

concepts.name: No inversion in a two-level system
concepts.statement: In a two-level atom the pump drives the lasing transition itself, raising atoms and stimulating their return at the same rate, so continuous pumping brings the upper population at most up to the lower one and never past it; such a laser could work only in jolts.

concepts.name: Three-level laser
concepts.statement: Pumping between the ground state and a third, upper level, the pair with the greatest energy difference, that decays into a metastable level of intermediate energy. Lasing then runs from the upper level to the metastable one, or from the metastable level to the ground state, at a frequency off-resonant with the pump, so the pump does not trigger stimulated emission.

concepts.name: Ruby laser
concepts.statement: Maiman's ruby laser, the first laser to operate: a three-level laser lasing from the metastable level of the Cr³⁺ ions in ruby to the ground state. A flash lamp must empty the ground state, so it lases in pulses: the lamp's light lasts about 1 ms and the laser pulse about 0.1 ms.

concepts.name: Transitions of a three-level system
concepts.statement: The nine events of a three-level system: absorption, spontaneous and stimulated emission between each pair of levels, each with its rate term such as ρ_ν(ν₁₃)B₁₃N₁ or A₃₂N₃. In most three-level lasers emission from level 3 to level 1 and absorption from level 1 to level 2 are negligible, which leaves at most five.

concepts.name: Inversion on the metastable level
concepts.statement: When spontaneous emission from the upper level into the metastable level is much faster than absorption or stimulated emission between them, the pumped atoms collect in the metastable level, and its population can exceed the ground state's: an inversion between levels 2 and 1.

concepts.name: Gain medium
concepts.statement: A collection of atoms or molecules that can attain a population inversion and so undergo stimulated emission and lase. It can be a gas, a liquid or a solid, a pure substance or a solution.

concepts.name: Steady state of a three-level laser
concepts.statement: At steady state each population is constant. For lasing from level 3 to level 2 the ratio N₃/N₂ follows from level 2's rate equation, and level 3 outnumbers level 2 when atoms in level 2 decay to the ground state faster than atoms in level 3 decay into level 2 (A₂₁ > A₃₂).

concepts.name: Four-level laser
concepts.statement: A laser whose lower lasing level is not the ground state, so it can be pumped more efficiently; He–Ne and Nd:YAG lasers are four-level lasers.

concepts.name: Optical cavity
concepts.statement: A pair of mirrors around the gain medium that feed its light back through it again and again, which is where the amplification happens. One mirror, the output coupler, reflects most of the light but lets a portion leave as the beam; the light trapped between the mirrors forms standing waves called modes.

concepts.name: Parts of a laser
concepts.statement: Most lasers have three parts: a gain medium that emits light of a specific frequency, a pump source that supplies its energy, and an optical cavity in which the light is amplified by passing through the medium again and again.

concepts.name: Continuous-wave and pulsed lasers
concepts.statement: A laser's beam is continuous or pulsed. Any laser can be pulsed by pumping it in regularly repeated bursts, but only a gain medium that can hold an inversion continuously gives a continuous-wave (CW) laser; the ruby laser cannot.

concepts.name: Exciplex laser
concepts.statement: A laser whose medium is an exciplex AB*, a gaseous species that exists only in an excited state: its lower, dissociated state holds no population, so the medium is inverted from the start, and the exciplex falls apart as it lases (XeCl* at 308 nm, KrF* at 249 nm). An excimer is an excited dimer AA*.

concepts.name: Dye laser
concepts.statement: A laser whose gain medium is an organic dye, usually in solution, passed through a cell or a jet. It can be tuned continuously over a wide range (rhodamine 6G from 560 to 635 nm) by a tuning element, often a movable diffraction grating.

concepts.name: Diode laser
concepts.statement: A semiconductor such as GaAs emits light when an electron and a hole recombine; removing the electrons that fall into the holes quickly keeps the inversion, and the crystal's high refractive index traps the light inside it. Doping changes the colour: GaAs emits infrared, GaAs₀.₆P₀.₄ red.

concepts.name: Excitation transfer from helium to neon
concepts.statement: Excited helium atoms in the metastable 2³S and 2¹S states, which cannot decay by radiating, give their energy to neon atoms in collisions, filling the neon levels of nearly the same energy, 2p⁵4s and 2p⁵5s.

concepts.name: Helium–neon laser
concepts.statement: The first continuous-wave laser: a four-level gas laser in which an electric discharge excites helium, helium hands its energy to neon's 4s and 5s levels, and neon lases down to its quickly emptied 4p and 3p levels, most often at 632.8 nm (5s → 3p); the mirrors choose the line. It gives a few mW, is very stable in wavelength and intensity, and runs near 0.1 % efficiency.

concepts.name: Laser spectroscopy
concepts.statement: Laser light's near monochromaticity, directionality and coherence make it a probe of atoms and molecules: one wavelength picks out one energy change, one component of a mixture or one quantum state, and a narrow, directed beam limits damage to the sample.

concepts.name: Time-resolved laser spectroscopy
concepts.statement: Short laser pulses follow reactions, biological processes and excited states over time, down to very short timescales.

concepts.name: Laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy
concepts.statement: A technique in which an intense laser turns a solid or liquid sample into a plasma, which is then probed.

concepts.name: Nonlinear spectroscopy
concepts.statement: High laser intensities make a sample behave in ways a weaker source cannot stimulate, which the nonlinear spectroscopies use.

concepts.name: Ideal gas
concepts.statement: An ideal gas is made of particles that exert no forces on each other; they feel a force only when they collide, elastically, with the walls of the container.

concepts.name: Pressure
concepts.statement: The mechanical definition of pressure is the average force exerted on a wall divided by the wall's area.

concepts.name: Pressure from wall collisions
concepts.statement: A particle that bounces elastically between walls a distance a apart pushes on a wall with the force mv_x²/a; summed over N particles in a cubic box, the pressure is Nm⟨v_x²⟩/a³.

concepts.name: Mean square velocity component
concepts.statement: From the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution, the average of the square of a molecule's velocity along x is k_BT/m.

concepts.name: Ideal gas law
concepts.statement: The pressure, volume and temperature of an ideal gas are related by PV = Nk_BT = nRT, which per mole reads P V̄ = RT.

concepts.name: Equation of state
concepts.statement: An equation of state is a relation between the variables that describes the state of matter under a set of given physical conditions, such as the relation between P, V and T.

concepts.name: Isotherm
concepts.statement: An isotherm is a graph of P against V at a fixed temperature; for an ideal gas the isotherms are hyperbolas.

concepts.name: Isochore
concepts.statement: An isochore is a graph of P against T at a fixed volume; for an ideal gas it is a straight line whose slope grows with the density.

concepts.name: An ideal gas never condenses
concepts.statement: An ideal gas can exist only as a gas: it cannot condense into an ideal liquid, so a phase transition from gas to liquid can be modeled only if the interactions between particles are accounted for.

concepts.name: Compressibility factor
concepts.statement: The compressibility factor Z = PV/nRT is 1 for an ideal gas at every pressure, so for a real gas it measures how far the gas deviates from ideal behavior.

concepts.name: Dilute gases behave ideally
concepts.statement: At sufficiently low pressures, and so low densities, every real gas approaches ideal-gas behavior: its compressibility factor goes to 1.

concepts.name: System and surroundings
concepts.statement: Thermodynamics divides the universe into a system and its surroundings with a boundary between them; the three together are the thermodynamic universe.

concepts.name: Extensive and intensive properties
concepts.statement: If a system is grown with the ratio N/V held constant, a property that grows with it is extensive (N, n, V, m, energy) and one that stays the same is intensive (P, ρ, T, molar heat capacity).

concepts.name: Molar volume
concepts.statement: The molar volume V̄ = V/n is the volume per mole, an intensive quantity.

concepts.name: Density
concepts.statement: The density ρ = N/V is the number of particles per unit volume, an intensive quantity.

concepts.name: Van der Waals equation of state
terms: van der Waals equation of state
concepts.statement: The van der Waals equation adjusts the ideal gas law for the nonzero volume of the molecules, through b, and for the attraction between them, through a; with a and b zero it reduces to PV = nRT.

concepts.name: Hard-sphere potential
concepts.statement: The hard-wall potential treats molecules as billiard balls of diameter σ: no force acts until their centres are σ apart, and they can come no closer.

concepts.name: Hard-sphere diameter
concepts.statement: The diameter σ of a hard sphere is the distance between the centres of two spheres at closest contact.

concepts.name: Van der Waals constant b
concepts.statement: The constant b is the volume excluded by a mole of molecules: two hard spheres exclude a sphere of radius σ, 4πσ³/3, half of it to each, so b = (2/3)πσ³N₀ and n moles leave a volume V − nb free.

concepts.name: Attraction lowers the pressure
concepts.statement: The net force on the wall is the force of the impacts less the attraction of the other molecules, so a real gas presses less than an ideal one; the correction an²/V² grows with the square of the density.

concepts.name: Van der Waals constant a
concepts.statement: The constant a measures the attraction between the molecules of a substance; it lowers the pressure by an²/V². Like b, it depends on the substance.

concepts.name: Cubic equation of state
concepts.statement: Van der Waals-type equations of state are cubic: cubic polynomials in the molar volume and in the compressibility factor.

concepts.name: Redlich–Kwong equation of state
concepts.statement: Redlich and Kwong (1949) made the attraction term of van der Waals depend on temperature, as a/√T, and put the co-volume b into its denominator; the equation is generally more accurate than van der Waals above the critical temperature.

concepts.name: Redlich–Kwong cubic in Z
concepts.statement: With A = aP/R²T^2.5 and B = bP/RT, the Redlich–Kwong equation becomes a cubic in the compressibility factor.

concepts.name: Redlich–Kwong constants
concepts.statement: Imposing the criticality conditions on the Redlich–Kwong equation ties a and b to the critical temperature and pressure of the substance.

concepts.name: Redlich–Kwong equation in reduced variables
concepts.statement: Written in P_r and T_r, the Redlich–Kwong cubic holds the same for every gas: any two gases at the same reduced pressure and temperature have the same compressibility factor.

concepts.name: Mixing rules
concepts.statement: A cubic equation of state is applied to a mixture as to a pseudo pure substance whose a and b are averages of the components' over their mole fractions.

concepts.name: The van der Waals loop
concepts.statement: Below the critical temperature a van der Waals isotherm turns S-shaped, with a stretch where P and V increase together; there the curve is no longer physical.

concepts.name: Tie line
concepts.statement: In reality the pressure stays constant between the liquid and gas ends of the loop; the horizontal tie line represents gas–liquid coexistence, at the vapor pressure of the liquid.

concepts.name: Maxwell's construction
concepts.statement: The tie line is placed so that the area between it and the isotherm above the line equals the area below it.

concepts.name: Critical point
concepts.statement: On the critical isotherm the tie line shrinks to a single point, the critical point, where liquid and vapor become the same and the isotherm has an inflection.

concepts.name: Critical temperature
concepts.statement: The critical temperature T_c is the one temperature at which the critical point exists, the highest at which a gas–liquid transition can occur.

concepts.name: Supercritical fluid
concepts.statement: Above the critical temperature there is no liquid–gas transition; the fluid resembles a liquid at higher pressures and a gas at lower ones.

concepts.name: Criticality conditions
concepts.statement: At the critical point the first and second derivatives of P with respect to V vanish.

concepts.name: Critical volume
concepts.statement: The critical volume V_c is the volume at the critical point.

concepts.name: Critical pressure
concepts.statement: The critical pressure P_c is the pressure at the critical point.

concepts.name: Van der Waals critical constants
concepts.statement: The criticality conditions applied to the van der Waals equation give V_c = 3nb, RT_c = 8a/27b and P_c = a/27b².

concepts.name: Roots of a cubic equation of state
concepts.statement: A cubic equation of state has one real root above the critical temperature, three equal roots at the critical point, and three real roots below it only for pressures across the S-shaped loop; the smallest is the liquid's molar volume, the largest the vapor's, and the middle one has no physical meaning.

concepts.name: Gas–liquid coexistence region
concepts.statement: The curve through the ends of the tie lines peaks at the critical point; inside it gas and liquid coexist.

concepts.name: Compressibility chart
concepts.statement: Standing and Katz's chart (1942) plots measured compressibility factors against pressure; graphical reading of such charts was widespread until computers.

concepts.name: Reduced variables
concepts.statement: The reduced pressure, volume and temperature measure a substance's state against its own critical point: P_r = P/P_c, V_r = V/V_c, T_r = T/T_c.

concepts.name: Van der Waals equation in reduced variables
concepts.statement: In reduced variables the van der Waals equation takes one universal form, with no constant of the substance left in it.

concepts.name: Law of corresponding states
concepts.statement: Different gases at the same reduced temperature and reduced pressure behave alike: two gases are in corresponding states when their reduced pressure, volume and temperature are the same.

concepts.name: Critical compressibility of a van der Waals gas
concepts.statement: The van der Waals equation gives Z = 3/8 at the critical point, which does not agree well with measurement.

concepts.name: Compressibility factor in reduced variables
concepts.statement: The van der Waals compressibility factor is a universal function of the reduced volume and temperature.

concepts.name: Generalized compressibility chart
concepts.statement: Measured Z of different fluids plotted against reduced pressure fall on one set of curves; simple hydrocarbons, noble gases and diatomic molecules conform closely, while strongly polar or hydrogen-bonded fluids such as water, ammonia and HF deviate.

concepts.name: Virial equation of state
concepts.statement: The virial equation of state expresses the deviation from ideality as a power series in the density, with the second, third, … virial coefficients as the coefficients.

concepts.name: Intermolecular pair potential
concepts.statement: The intermolecular pair potential is the potential energy of two molecules as a function of their separation.

concepts.name: Mayer f-function
concepts.statement: The Mayer f-function, exp(−Φ₁₂/k_BT) − 1, is zero where the pair potential vanishes, −1 where it is infinitely repulsive and positive where it is attractive.

concepts.name: Configuration integral
concepts.statement: A configuration integral Z_j integrates the Boltzmann factor of the interaction energy of j molecules over all their positions; Z₁ = V.

concepts.name: Second virial coefficient
concepts.statement: The second virial coefficient gives the contribution of the pair potential to the pressure, the initial departure from ideal-gas behavior; it is an integral of the Mayer f-function over the separation.

forms.latex: B_{2}= \dfrac{1}{2} \iint v_{\mathrm {excluded}} (\Omega,\Omega') f(\Omega) f(\Omega')~ {\mathrm d}\Omega {\mathrm d}\Omega'

concepts.name: Second virial coefficient of hard spheres
concepts.statement: For hard spheres of diameter σ, B₂ = 2πσ³/3, independent of temperature.

concepts.name: Isihara–Hadwiger formula
concepts.statement: For any hard convex body, B₂ = RS + V exactly, where V is its volume, S its surface area and R its mean radius of curvature.

concepts.name: Second virial coefficient of a van der Waals gas
concepts.statement: For the van der Waals equation of state, B₂ = b − a/RT: the excluded volume raises it and the attraction lowers it, more so the colder the gas.

concepts.name: Lennard-Jones potential
concepts.statement: The Lennard-Jones potential describes the potential energy of two nonbonding atoms or molecules against their separation: a steep r⁻¹² repulsive term and a smoother r⁻⁶ attractive term.

concepts.name: Lennard-Jones σ
concepts.statement: σ is the separation at which the Lennard-Jones potential is zero, a measure of how close two nonbonding particles can get.

concepts.name: Van der Waals radius
concepts.statement: The van der Waals radius is one-half of the internuclear distance between nonbonding particles, σ/2.

concepts.name: Kinds of intermolecular attraction
concepts.statement: Neutral molecules attract one another through dipole–dipole, dipole–induced dipole and London (dispersion) interactions.

concepts.name: Repulsion and attraction in the Lennard-Jones potential
concepts.statement: Far apart, two particles barely interact; brought closer they attract and become bound, down to an equilibrium separation; pressed closer still, their electrons are forced into each other's orbitals and the repulsion soars.

concepts.name: Forces along the Lennard-Jones curve
concepts.statement: A particle feels a repulsive force closer than the equilibrium distance r_min, an attractive force beyond it and no force at it, slightly beyond σ, where the potential is at its minimum and the pair is most stable.

concepts.name: Evaluating the Lennard-Jones potential
concepts.statement: Given ε, σ and a separation r, substitute into V(r) = 4ε[(σ/r)¹² − (σ/r)⁶] to find the intermolecular potential, and read off from σ whether it should be positive or negative.

concepts.name: Virial expansion of the van der Waals equation
concepts.statement: Expanding 1/(1 − b/V̄) as a series turns the van der Waals equation into a virial series whose second coefficient is b − a/RT.

concepts.name: Dispersion coefficient C₆
concepts.statement: C₆ is the strength of the intermolecular attraction that falls off as r⁻⁶.

concepts.name: Hard sphere with an r⁻⁶ attraction
concepts.statement: Combining the hard sphere with the attractive part of the Lennard-Jones potential gives an infinite wall at σ and −C₆/r⁶ beyond it.

concepts.name: Van der Waals constants from molecular parameters
concepts.statement: For hard spheres with an r⁻⁶ attraction, B₂ takes the van der Waals form b − a/RT with b = (2/3)πN₀σ³, four times the volume of the molecules, and a proportional to C₆: van der Waals assumes hard spheres at small distances and weak attractions at larger ones.

concepts.name: Newton's second law
concepts.statement: Particles move under the forces they exert on each other and any external fields: each particle's mass times its acceleration equals the force on it, m_i r̈_i = F_i(r_1, …, r_N).

concepts.name: Force field
concepts.statement: The forces on the particles, written as functions of all the particle positions, F_i(r_1, …, r_N), are known as a force field.

concepts.name: Trajectories from initial conditions
concepts.statement: Newton's equations for N particles are 3N coupled second-order differential equations; given the initial positions and velocities, their solution gives every coordinate and velocity for all time.

concepts.name: Temperature and kinetic energy
concepts.statement: The temperature is set by the average kinetic energy of the particles: (3/2)NkT equals the sum of ½m_iv_i² over the N particles.

concepts.name: Many microscopic states, one macroscopic state
concepts.statement: Specifying the trajectory of some 10²³ particles would take essentially infinite information, but the detail is not needed: enormous numbers of microscopic states give rise to the same macroscopic observable, such as the same temperature.

concepts.name: Ensemble
concepts.statement: An ensemble is a large collection of systems described by the same microscopic forces and sharing the same macroscopic thermodynamic variables, such as total energy, number of moles and volume, each evolving from a different initial condition.

concepts.name: Ensemble concept
concepts.statement: Macroscopic observables can be calculated by averaging over the systems of an ensemble; for time-independent properties such as temperature and pressure the average may be taken at one instant.

concepts.name: Thermal energy
concepts.statement: Boltzmann looked at temperature as a form of energy: the thermal energy of a system is directly proportional to the absolute temperature, E_thermal = kT.

concepts.name: Boltzmann constant
concepts.statement: The Boltzmann constant k (or k_B) is the proportionality constant between thermal energy and absolute temperature, and plays a central role in all of statistical thermodynamics.

concepts.name: Thermodynamic beta
concepts.statement: β is the reciprocal of the thermal energy, 1/kT.

concepts.name: Boltzmann factor
concepts.statement: The Boltzmann factor e^(−βE_i) of a state of energy E_i, with β = 1/kT, approximates the fraction of particles of a large system that are in that state.

concepts.name: Activation energy
concepts.statement: The activation energy is the energy a particle must carry to cross the energy barrier of an activation process.

concepts.name: Activated processes follow the Boltzmann factor
concepts.statement: The rates of many physical processes are set by the Boltzmann factor: the fraction of particles with enough energy to cross an activation barrier, such as escaping a surface, is about proportional to it, so a higher temperature sends more particles across.

concepts.name: Canonical ensemble
concepts.statement: The canonical ensemble holds N, V and T fixed: a collection of boxes of equal volume and number of particles, the whole collection kept in thermal equilibrium. It is the most practical ensemble.

concepts.name: Occupation number
concepts.statement: In an ensemble of A systems, a_j is the number of systems in quantum state j; the set a_1, a_2, … is a distribution.

concepts.name: Weight of a distribution
concepts.statement: The number of microstates that realize a distribution a_1, a_2, … of A systems over the quantum states is W = A!/(a_1!a_2!…).

concepts.name: Ensemble average
concepts.statement: The probability P_j that a system is in state j is the average of a_j/A over the allowed distributions, and any thermodynamic property is the average ⟨M⟩ = Σ_j M_jP_j.

concepts.name: Method of the most probable distribution
concepts.statement: A system tends toward the distribution of a_j that maximizes the number of microstates W, and with so many particles the fluctuations from the mean are immeasurably small, so the average distribution is this most probable one.

concepts.name: Constraints on a distribution
concepts.statement: A distribution must conserve energy, E_total = Σ_j a_je_j, and the number of systems, A = Σ_j a_j.

concepts.name: Method of Lagrange multipliers
concepts.statement: The method of Lagrange multipliers finds the local maxima and minima of a function subject to equality constraints by adding each constraint times an undetermined multiplier.

concepts.name: Stirling's approximation
concepts.statement: For large x, ln x! is approximately x ln x − x.

concepts.name: Probability of a state in the Boltzmann distribution
concepts.statement: Maximizing W while the energy and the number of systems stay fixed gives the most probable distribution, a thermally equilibrated distribution over all energy levels: the fraction of systems in state j is P_j = e^(−βe_j)/Σ_j e^(−βe_j).

concepts.name: Lower states hold more molecules
concepts.statement: In the Boltzmann distribution a state of lower energy always has a higher population than one of higher energy, and above absolute zero every upper level has a non-zero population however large the spacing; at higher temperatures more of the upper states are populated, each less.

concepts.name: Molecular partition function
concepts.statement: The molecular partition function is the sum of the Boltzmann factors over the states of one molecule, q = Σ_j e^(−βe_j); it is a number.

concepts.name: The partition function counts accessible states
concepts.statement: The molecular partition function indicates the average number of states thermally accessible to a molecule at the temperature of the system: the larger q, the more states the molecule can occupy.

concepts.name: Canonical partition function
concepts.statement: The partition function of the ensemble, Q(N, V, T), sums the Boltzmann factors over every state accessible to the system, counting every combination of the occupations of the molecules' states.

concepts.name: Partition function of distinguishable, independent molecules
concepts.statement: For independent molecules that can be told apart, the partition function of the system is the product of the molecular ones, Q = q_iq_jq_k…, which is Q = q^N when every molecule has the same states.

concepts.name: Partition function of indistinguishable molecules
concepts.statement: If the molecules cannot be told apart, q^N counts N! states too many, since N! is how many times the indices can be swapped without changing anything; the partition function is then Q = q^N/N!.

concepts.name: Average ensemble energy
concepts.statement: The average energy is each energy times its Boltzmann probability, summed: ⟨E⟩ = Σ_i E_iP_i = Σ_i E_ie^(−E_i/kT)/Q. It is the observed energy of the system.

concepts.name: Average energy from the partition function
concepts.statement: The average energy is a derivative of ln Q: ⟨E⟩ = kT²(∂ln Q/∂T) = −(∂ln Q/∂β).

concepts.name: Internal energy
concepts.statement: The internal energy U is the energy of the system, which statistical mechanics computes as the average ensemble energy.

concepts.name: Heat capacity at constant volume
concepts.statement: The heat capacity at constant volume is the change in internal energy with temperature, C_V = (∂U/∂T)_{N,V}.

concepts.name: Heat capacity from the partition function
concepts.statement: The heat capacity at constant volume is a second derivative of ln Q with respect to β: C_V = (1/kT²)∂²ln Q/∂β² = kβ²∂²ln Q/∂β².

concepts.name: Dulong–Petit law
concepts.statement: Dulong and Petit found in 1819 that solids have a heat capacity of about 2.49 × 10⁴ J kmol⁻¹ K⁻¹ near room temperature, explained by treating each atom as an oscillator with six degrees of freedom: C_V = 6R/2 = 3R.

concepts.name: Heat capacities fall toward zero at low temperature
concepts.statement: Experiment shows that the heat capacity of a solid decreases as the temperature approaches absolute zero, which the Dulong–Petit law cannot explain.

concepts.name: Einstein model of a solid
concepts.statement: Einstein treated a solid of N atoms as 3N independent oscillators: each atom moves in three dimensions within the lattice, the atoms do not interact, and all of them vibrate at the same frequency ν.

concepts.name: Einstein temperature
concepts.statement: The Einstein temperature Θ_E = hν/k writes the oscillator frequency ν of the atoms in a solid as a temperature.

concepts.name: Einstein heat capacity
concepts.statement: In Einstein's model the heat capacity of a solid is C_V = 3Nk(Θ_E/T)²e^(Θ_E/T)/(e^(Θ_E/T) − 1)², set by how accessible the vibrational energy is at the temperature T.

concepts.name: High-temperature limit of the Einstein heat capacity
concepts.statement: When the temperature is very large compared with the Einstein temperature, C_V ≈ 3Nk = 3nR, the value of Dulong and Petit.

concepts.name: Low-temperature limit of the Einstein heat capacity
concepts.statement: When the temperature is small compared with the Einstein temperature, C_V ≈ 3Nk(Θ_E/T)²e^(−Θ_E/T), which goes to zero with T, as experiment shows.

concepts.name: Stiff, light solids have low heat capacities
concepts.statement: Since ν = (1/2π)√(κ/μ), a solid with a high force constant or a low reduced mass, such as diamond, has a high Einstein temperature, and its heat capacity stays low until the temperature is high.

concepts.name: Where the Einstein model falls short
concepts.statement: Einstein's model fits the heat capacity of a solid at high temperatures, but at the lowest temperatures (below about 15 K for lead) it departs from experiment: the atoms of a real solid interact, which Debye's model takes up.

concepts.name: Pressure of a state
concepts.statement: The pressure of a system in state i is the negative change of that state's energy with volume, P_i = −(∂E_i/∂V)_N.

concepts.name: Pressure from the partition function
concepts.statement: The average pressure is a derivative of ln Q with respect to volume: ⟨P⟩ = kT(∂ln Q/∂V)_{N,β}.

concepts.name: Translational partition function
concepts.statement: The translational partition function of a molecule of mass m in a volume V is q = (2πm/h²β)^{3/2}V.

concepts.name: Gas constant
concepts.statement: R, the universal gas constant (8.314 J/mol-K), is Boltzmann's constant multiplied by Avogadro's number, N_Ak = R; it converts from a per-molecule to a per-mole basis, so Nk = nR.

concepts.name: Pressure as the energy change with volume
concepts.statement: A system pushing on a piston of area A exerts the force F = dE/dz; since A dz = −dV, the pressure is P = −dE/dV.

concepts.name: Classical canonical partition function
concepts.statement: For classical particles the canonical partition function is an integral of e^(−β𝓔(x)) over every point x of phase space, 𝓔(x) being the mechanical energy there; for N identical particles the integral carries the factor 1/(N!h^{3N}).

concepts.name: Canonical partition function of an ideal gas
concepts.statement: Evaluating the Gaussian integrals over the momenta gives the canonical partition function of an ideal gas, Q(N, V, T) = (1/N!)[(V/h³)(2πm/β)^{3/2}]^N.

concepts.name: Energies of independent molecules add
concepts.statement: The energy of a system of independent molecules is the sum of their energies, each molecule in its own state: E_l = ε_i^a + ε_j^b + ε_k^c + ⋯.

concepts.name: Distinguishable molecules
concepts.statement: Molecules are distinguishable when each can be told apart from the others, as the molecules of a crystal can be by the fixed sites they move around.

concepts.name: Two particles on two levels
concepts.statement: Two particles on the levels 0 and ε have four states if they can be told apart, Q = 1 + 2e^(−βε) + e^(−2βε) = q², but only three if they cannot, Q = 1 + e^(−βε) + e^(−2βε), which is not q².

concepts.name: When dividing by N! works
concepts.statement: Dividing q^N by N! counts the states of indistinguishable molecules only approximately, well when they rarely share a state, as in a large system with many accessible states; for two particles on two levels q²/2 is not the true partition function.

concepts.name: Average energy of a molecule
concepts.statement: The average energy of a single particle is its energies weighted by their Boltzmann probabilities, ⟨ε⟩ = Σ_i ε_ie^(−ε_i/kT)/q.

concepts.name: Average energy of independent molecules
concepts.statement: For N independent, indistinguishable molecules the average energy is N times that of one molecule: ⟨E⟩ = NkT²(∂ln q/∂T)_V = N⟨ε⟩.

concepts.name: Energy of a molecule by degree of freedom
concepts.statement: The energy of a molecule is the sum of the energies of its degrees of freedom: ε = ε_trans + ε_rot + ε_vib + ε_elec.

concepts.name: Molecular partition function as a product
concepts.statement: Because the energy of a molecule is a sum over its degrees of freedom, its partition function is the product of theirs: q = q_trans q_rot q_vib q_elec.

concepts.name: Partition function of a degree of freedom
concepts.statement: Each degree of freedom has its own partition function, a sum of Boltzmann factors over its states such as q_vib = Σ_i e^(−ε_i/kT), and its own average energy, ⟨ε_vib⟩ = kT²∂ln q_vib/∂T = −∂ln q_vib/∂β.

concepts.name: Translational levels of a gas particle in a cube
concepts.statement: A monatomic gas particle in a cubic box of length L has the translational energies E = h²(n_x² + n_y² + n_z²)/8mL², with quantum numbers n_x, n_y and n_z in the three directions.

concepts.name: Translational partition function as a product over directions
concepts.statement: Because the energy is a sum over the three directions, the translational partition function is the product of the partition functions for each direction, q_trans = q_x q_y q_z.

concepts.name: Sum over closely spaced levels as an integral
concepts.statement: When the levels are very closely spaced, nearly continuous on the scale of kT, a partition function's sum over them can be replaced by an integral; the lower limit may then be extended to zero.

concepts.name: Translational partition function in one dimension
concepts.statement: For one direction of a box of length L, the sum over n_x becomes a Gaussian integral and q_x = ½√(π/a) with a = h²/8mL²kT, or q_x = L/Λ.

concepts.name: Thermal de Broglie wavelength
concepts.statement: The length Λ = h/√(2πmkT), which the book calls the de Broglie wavelength of the particle; a box of length L holds L/Λ translational states per direction within reach at temperature T.

concepts.name: Many translational states are accessible
concepts.statement: The translational partition function is a very large number for a gas in an ordinary volume, so a very large number of translational states are thermally accessible, far more than there are molecules.

concepts.name: Electronic partition function
concepts.statement: The sum over the electronic levels of each level's degeneracy times its Boltzmann factor, q_el = g₁e^(−E₁/kT) + g₂e^(−E₂/kT) + ….

forms.latex: q_{elec}(T) = g_1 + g_2 e^{-E_2/kT} + g_3 e^{-E_3/kT} + \ldots

concepts.name: A degenerate level counts once per state
concepts.statement: A level of degeneracy g holds g states at one energy, so in a partition function its Boltzmann factor is multiplied by g.

concepts.name: Most atoms are in the ground electronic state
concepts.statement: Electronic states typically lie tens of thousands of wavenumbers above the ground state, far more than kT, so the excited states are not accessible at ordinary temperatures and q_elec is the ground level's degeneracy, often 1.

concepts.name: Partition function of a molecular ideal gas
concepts.statement: With the molecule's partition function written as q_trans q_vib q_rot q_elec, the partition function of an ideal gas of N molecules is Q = (q_trans q_vib q_rot q_elec)^N/N!.

concepts.name: Finding a heat capacity from energy levels
concepts.statement: To find a degree of freedom's contribution: define its energy states and degeneracies, compose q for the molecule and Q for the gas, take the β or T derivative of ln Q for ⟨E⟩, and take the T derivative of U ≈ ⟨E⟩ for the heat capacity.

concepts.name: Geometric series
concepts.statement: For |x| < 1, the series 1 + x + x² + x³ + … sums to 1/(1 − x).

concepts.name: Vibrational partition function
concepts.statement: Summing the Boltzmann factors of a diatomic's harmonic levels (v + ½)hν as a geometric series gives q_vib = e^(−hν/2kT)/(1 − e^(−hν/kT)); measured from the ground level it is 1/(1 − e^(−hν/kT)).

forms.latex: q_\text{vib} = \dfrac{e^{-h \nu / 2 k T}} {1 - e^{-h \nu/ k T}}

concepts.name: Vibrational temperature
concepts.statement: The temperature Θ_vib = hcν̃/k = hν/k that expresses the stiffness of a vibrating bond in units of the Boltzmann constant; each normal mode of a polyatomic molecule has its own.

concepts.name: What sets the vibrational temperature
